THE WHIP-POOR-WILL. Why dost thou come at set of sun, Those pensive words to say? Why Whip-poor-Will? What has he done? And who is Will, I pray? Why come from you leaf-shaded hill, A suppliant at my door? Why ask of me to Whip poor Will? And is Will really poor ? , If poverty's his crime, let mirth ' From out his heart be driven; That seem* the deadliest sin on earth, And never is forgiven. Art Will himself? it must be so. I learn it from thy moan, For none can feel another's woe. As deeply as his own. Yet wherefore strain thy tiny throat, While other birds repose? What means thy melancholy note? The mystery disclose. Still Whip-poor-Will ?—Art thou a spirit From unknown regions sent, To wa,cler in the gloom of night, . And ask for punishment? ' Art thou It low; Will? East proved The fairest can deceive ' Thine is the lot of all who've loved, Since Adam wedded Eve. • East trusted in a friend, and seen • No friend was he in need? A common error—men still lean Upon as frail a reed. Has thou, in seeking wealth or fame, A crown of brambles won? O'er all the earth 'tis just the same With every mother's son! East found the:world a Babel wide, Where man to mammon stoops? Where flourish arrogance and pride, While modest merit droops? What, none of these? Then whence thy pain? To guess it who's the skill? Pray have the kindness to explain Why I should Whip poor Will. , Dost merely ask thy just dessert? What! not another word ? ' Back to the woods again, unhurt; I will not harm thee, bird. I'll treat thee kindly, for my nerves, Like thine, have penance done. Treat every man as he deserves— Who shall 'scape whipping? None. Farewell, poor Will—not valueless This lesson by thee given; "Keep thine own counsel, and confess Thyself alone to Heaven." The foregoing lines are from the pen of General Morris, long a resident on the banks of the Hudson River, and who conducted one of the New York literary journals. The poem happily expresses the train of thought natu- rally excited by the mourning strain of the bird.

"To live long," says Cicero, "it is necessary to live slowly." Telegraph messenger boys keep this saying pasted in their hats. "What are the last teeth that come?" asked a Lynn teacher to her class in physiology. "Jralse teeth, mum," replied boy who had just waked up on the back seat. "I beg your pardon, sir, but is not your name Smythe?" Second gentleman: "No, sir; my name is Smith. You have undoubtedly mistaken me for my son." Englishman: "Is land dear in Japan ?"—Japanese "No, but the ground rents are awful."—Englishman: "What is the cause of that ?"—Japanese: "Earth- quakes." - A visitor in Dublin was asked by a car-driver if he wantgd a car. "No," said he, "I am able to walk." "May your honour long be able, but seldom willing," was the witty rejoinder. The Earl of Carnarvon, at a banquet, in proposing "The health of the clergy," said that "in these days clergymen were expected to have the wisdom and learn-, ing of a Jeremy Taylor." His lordship was next day reported to have said, "in these days clergymen were expected to have the wisdom and learning of a journey- man tailor."

The quierrelsome man not only poisons the happiness of his family and friends, but also his own. Ile generates ; antagonism, illfeeling' and dislike wherever he vents his I spleen, and these react on him to his misery. When to this is added the internal irritation of his own feeling, it is very certain that he is himself the greatest sufferer from his own pugnacity. Tramp; to gentleman in St. James's Park: "Will you kindly allow me to glance at your paper for a moment, sir? I am anxious to see the weather predictions." Gentleman, handing him the paper: "Certainly. Are you interested in the weather?" Tramp: "Yes, sir. I live principally on wind, and I want to find out what I'm to have for dinner to-day." "

UNAITTHORISED'ITEM.-At a Parisian restaurant a patron complains of the amount of the bill. "But what am I to do ?" says the host, with a sweeping gesture. "You can't have magnificent mirrors and rich orna- ments like these unless you pay for them. You can't have frescoes and genuine gilt for nothing." The patron responds phlegmatically, "Let the waiter remove them then; I didn't order them. • _ _ _ _ _

Benevolence has a farther,reaching service to render to mankind than is usually supposed. Not merely to listen to complaints, to relieve conscious suffering, and to supply recognised deficiences is her appointed work, but also to detect the poverty that fancies itself rich, the ignorance that thinks itself wise, the grievances suffered unknowingly, the wrongs inflicted unthinkingly, the sins committed without remorse, the woes endured with effort to avert them. THE QUEEN'S DAIJOHTER.—A good many years ago, when her Majesty was spending a short time in the neighbourhood of Trossachs, the Princesses Louise and Beatrice paid an unexpected visit to an old female cot- tager on the slopes of Glenfinlas, who, knowing that they had some connection with the Royal household, bluntly ,ejaculated, " Ye'll be the Queen's servants, I'm think- in' ?" "No." they quietly rejoined; "we are the Queen's daughters." "Ye dinna look like it," was the imme- diate reply of the unusually outspoken Celt, "as ye hae neither a ring on your fingers nor a bit gowd your lugs!" 1 A man had a story about a gun which he delivered himself of upon all occasions. At a dinner party one evening he writhed in his chair for over an hour waiting lor a chance to introduce his story, but no opportunity presented itself, Finally he slipped a coin into the hand of a waiter, and whispered, "When you leave the room again, slam the door." The waiter slammed the door as directed, and the man sprang to his feet with the ex- aamation, "What's that noise—a gun?" "Oh, no," resumed his host, "it was only the door." "Ah, I see. Well, speaking of guns, reminds me of a little story." Curran used to relate with great glee a mishap which befell a Roman Catholic Bishop who went up to Dublin Castle to adulate the Ird Lieutenant. It seems that one of Lord Ceruvralli,?s eyes was smaller than the other, and had acquired a quick, perpetually oscillating motion. , The addreese,rs, who had never seen him, had elaborated their caurpliments on the country. His Excellency was on his t!arone in high state, when Bishop Lanigan of Kit- kern,., at the head of his clergy, commenced, " Your Excilencey has always kept a steady eye upon the inter- r.,ts of England." The room was in a roar. "Never," said Curran, "did I hear its match, except in the Mayor of Coventry's compliment to Queen Elizabeth—' When the Spanish Armada attacked your Majesty, they caught the wrong sow by the ear." Dr. Samuel Wilberforce, when Bishop of Oxford, while paying a visit at Taymouth Castle during the life-time of the last Marquis of Breadalbane, a devoted adherent of the Free Church, was taken by Lady Breadalbane into: one of the cottages on the estate occupied by an old High- land woman—a "true blue" Presbyterian—who was greatly pleased at the bishop's frank and friendly manner. A few days afterwards the bishop left the 1 castle, and Lady Breadalbane paid another visit to her old friend, when the following conversation took place— 'Do you know who that was, Mary, that came to see you ast week?" 't No, my lady," was the reply. "The famous Bishop of Oxford," said her ladyship. On which the old Presbyterian remarked, " Aweel, my lady, he's a rate fine Man; and a' I can say is that I trust and pray he'll gang to heeven, bishop though he be." When has a man four hands ?—When he doubles his fists. Pure minds—to be good company for yourself, you must store your mind well; fill it with happy and pure thoughts, with pleasant memories of the past and reason- able hopes for the future. You must, so far as may be, Protect yourself from self-reproach, from care, and from anxiety. Be careful, then, how you choose your thoughts. You cannot keep your minds pure if you allow them to dwell on detailed accounts of crime and sin; the soul is dyed by its thoughts. Peace of mind, as Ruskin beauti- fully observes, must come in its own time, as the waters settle themselves into clearness as well as quietness; you can no more filter your mind into purity than you can compress it into calmness; you must keep it pure if you would have it pure, and throw no stones into it if you would have it quiet. It is not isolated great deeds which do most to form a character, but small conterminous acts touching and blending into one another. The greenness of a field eomes not from trees, but from blades of grass. When illicit distilling was common in Aberdeenshire, there was at one time an old man who went about the country repairing whisky-pots. The gauger, meeting him one day, guessing that he had been doing some repairs at no great distance, asked what he would take to in- form him—the gauger—where he repaired the last whisky-pot, " Och," said Donald, "she'll shust tak half. a-croon !", Very well," said the gauger, "here is your money; but be careful to tell me correctly." A LLSSON WITH A MORAL.
'HEN WILL OUR EYES BE OPENED TO THIS GREAT NATIONAL CALAMITY.

I The year 1886 played sad havoc with many prominent men of our country. Many of them died without warning, passing away appar- ently in the full flush of life. Others were sick but a comparatively short time. We turn to our files and are astonished to find that most of them died of apoplexy, of paralysis, of nervous prostration, Of malignant blood humour, of Bright's disease, of heart disease, of kidney disease, of rheumatism, or of pneumonia. It is singular that most of our prominent men die of these disordirs. Any journalist who watches the telegraph re- Ports, Will be astonished at the number of prominent vic- tim's of these disorders. Many statements have appeared in our paper with others, le the effect that the diseases that carried off so many . pro Minent men in 1886, are really one disease, taking different names according to the location of the fatal effects. When a valuable horse perishes, it becomes the nine days talk of the sporting world, and yet thousands of ordinary horses are dying every day. Their aggregate less is enor- Mous, and yet their death creates no comment. So it is with individuals. The cause of death of promi- nent men creates comment, especially when it can be shown that one unsuspected disease carries off most of them, and 'Yet " vast numbers of ordinary men and women die before their time every year from the same cause." it Is said if the blood Is kept free from uric acid, that heart disease, paralysis, nervous prostration, pneumonia, rheumatism, and many cases of consumption, would sever be known. This uric acid, we are told, is the waste Of the system, and it is the duty of the kidneys to remove this waste. We are told that if the kidneys are maintained in perfect oealth, the uric, kidney., acid is kept out of the blood, and Lhese sudden and universal diseases caused by uric acid will large measure disappear. 'nut how shall this be done ? It is folly to treat effects. If there is any known way of getting at the cause, that • Way should be known to the public. We believe that 14 Warner's SAFE Cure;' of which so much has been written, and 80 much talked of by the public generally, is now re- cognised by impartial physicians and the public as the one Specific for such diseases. Because public attention has been directed to this great remedy by means of advertising, some persons have not be- lieved in the remedy. We cannot see how Mr. Warner

could immediately benefit the public in any other way, and his valuable specific should not be condemned because some nostrums have come before the public in the same way, any More than that all doctors should be condemned because so many of them are incompetent. It is astonishing what good opinions you hear on every aide, of this great remedy, and public opinion thus based uDon an actual experience, has all the weight and impor- tance of absolute truth. At this time of the year, the uric acid in the blood invites Pneumonia, and rheumatism, and there is not a man who 'cl°sB not dread these monsters of disease; but he need have fear of them if la) rid the blood of the uric acid cause. 4413 can be done with " Warner's SAFE Cure," which can be Prneured of all chemists and medicine vendors at 4u6d Pr bottle, or direct of the proprietor, H. div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoNDAL

, The Speaker took the chair at 4 p.m. THE BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE ANT, HOLIDATS.—MT. W. H. Sitrrn, in reply to Mr. Pickersgill, said that the-Go- vernment Were most anxious to bonsiderthe.convenience of the House, but they felt it to be their duty to sal the House to read the Criminal Law Amendment Bill a second time before they proposed the usual Bastes holi- days. The Government disavowed any menace, but he wished the House to understand that the measure which the Government proposed, which was vital to the main- tenance of order in Ireland, and on which the Govern- ment staked their own existence, was even nsore,imper- tent than the usual holiday, however much it might be needed.

THE BELPAsT IltoTs.—Mr. HEALY having put a ques- tion to the Attorney-General for Ireland about the trial of the Walkers (father and son) for murders during the Belfast riots, and received an answer, said: I beg to give notice that I shall, on the earliest possible oppor- tunity, call attention to the scandalous conduct of the Crown with reference—The SPEAKER: The hon. mem- ber is well aware that these terms would not be permit- ted in a question on the paper. (Ministerial cheers.) —Mr. HEALY : Then I shall call attention to the conduct of the Government in reference to the trial of these two men, and I shall charge them with deliberately conniving at the escape of these two murderers. (Panaellite cheers.)
THE COERCION BILL EXTRAORDINARY PROPOSALS.

Mr. A. J. BALvcitm moved the first reading of the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill. Hassid there was an amendment on the paper standing in the name of Mr. Parnell, which invited the House to obtain farther

information with respect to the,condition of Ireland; but he thought the House had sufficient information, and •that the Irish members should recognise that, as an artificer recognises his own work. The Government did not rest their case for special restrictive legislation on the statistics of agrarian crime. They took the view adopted by, Mr. Gladstone, that account must be had, not only of the amount of crime, but of the amount in conjunction with its cause and character, what it indicated and what it meant. In only seven years since 1845 had the amount of 'crime in Ireland stood higher than it oid now, and in every one of those years exceptional legislation was introduced. The amount of the crime and the failure of the law might be judged from the fact that at this moment 498 persons in Mun- ster. 175 in Connaught, 251 in Leinster, and 23 in Ulster, were under police protection. The number of police required to carry out the special protection afforded was 770, and some idea of the initial cost thrown upon the ratepayers of -this country by the maintenance of this protection might be gathered from the fact that each policeman cost on the average £7O, and that the total cost, therefore, for extra police was no less a sum than £55,000 a-year. The 'law had ,been set aside, and the vacuum left bad not been filled by the ordinary law, by the law of the Crown or of Parliament, but by an unwritten law. He read at length from the charges of the judges to the grand juries at the winter assizes, to show that the num- ber of .persons actually charged bore no relation to the amount of ,crime; that boycotting, intimidation, and so forth were rampant, and remained unpunished; andthat the country was in a most disturbed condition. The men who gave that testimony were not partisans. A more terrible picture of society never was drawn than was given in those charges. The paralysis of the courts of law was the evil specially to be dealt with, and it arose from the fact that evidence to convict was not forthcoming. In 755 cases, no fewer than 422 of the injured parties were so terrified by the system of intimi- dation which prevailed that they would not come for- ward and give evidence. Mr. PARNELL : Are you taking the number of agrarian I offences, or do you Include all offences committed in the I districts to which your statistics refer? Mr. BALFOUR: The returns give the number of grave offences.

_ . Mr. PARNBLI.: Are they agrarian? Mr. BALFotru : No, they are not all agrarian. (Par- nellite laughter and cheers.) But with regard to this question, I may say that the interruption of the honour= able memher for Cork was a relevant one, but as t• the words, "gave offences," used in the statistics, I should say that the pOlice have unduly restricted the cases they describe as agrarian. (Parnellite laughter.) I make this observation in order to put honourable gentlemen right in respect to their statistics • but my case is that the whole of this part of Ireland is now in a state of total disorganisation. (Ministerial cheers.) I decline absplutely to restrict my attention to agrarian offences. (Ministerial cheers and derisive Opposition cheers.) And I say this, that if in 422 cases where injuries are inflicted those who are injured de not dare to come° forward to give ,evidcrice it matters not whether the crime is agrarian or not, it shows that there is a condi- tion of terrorism existing with which this liouseis bound to deal without delay. (Ministerial cheers:) Another cause of the paralysis of the course of the law is the fact that even when evidence is forthcoming juries, in the faee of the clearest possible evidence, decline altogethtr to convict. (" Rear, hoar," from the Parnellite benches.) That cheer from the hon. member for Longford shows that the hon. member fully approves of this conduct on the part of Irish juries. (Ministerial cheers.) Mr. T. HEALY : I deny the assertion altogether. (Par- nellite cheers.) Mr. BALFOUR proceeded to give instances of the con- duct of the juries •in the county of Roscommon, and citing trial in which although the evidence against priso- .ners was held to beconclusive, verdicts of acquittal were returned.

Dr. TAt,NER Might I say a word? The SPEAKER: I shall And it very difficult to 'conduct the debate without the co-operation of the House. the honourable member will have an opportunity to reply at The proper time. (Ministerial cheers.) Mr. BALFOUR, having enumerated further instances of refusal on the part of-juries to convict, and having quoted largely from the speeches of Irish members in connection with meetings.of the National League held to organise and carry out the system of.boycotting and in- timidation, said he apprehended the House would he satisfied that the jury -system in Ireland was unworkable. The place that the law ought to fulfil was occupied by the National League. The league relied on dark and secret societies, dynamite, and the dagger, whose object was anarchy, and whose means were assassination. Taking into con- sideration the public utterances, he contended it was an absurd-travesty of facts to say that the National League had any resemblance to trades unionism, which existed only for the protection of the weak. The speeches of the Nationalists were enforced by a mode of intimida- tion painfully familiar to the House. As to the difficulty in getting-verdicts, he proposed to abolish the trial by jury system altogether. For certain classes of crime two magistrates should have jurisdiction, and a maxi-e mum power of six months' imprisonment for the follow- ing offences :—Criminal conspiracy, boycotting, rioting, offences against the Whitehoy Acts, assaulting officers of the law, forcible and unlawful possession, and inciting to the above offences. The Government did not propose to interfere with the liberty of the press, but they enter- tained a hope ,that, by giving power of summary con- viction for inciting to these offences, they might be able to prevent the press from havingashare in these crimes. The bill gave ,power to the. High Court to change the venue. The •Government felt the difficulty of abolishing trial by jury for the graver offences. They preferred to retain the jury system so long as it could be applied so as to get a verdict. They therefore proposed that the Attorney-Generals for England and Ireland together should certify theta fairer trial could be had in England, and then, under the same condition as to changing the venue in Ireland, the trial should be held in England. The bill also provided that Irish counsel should be allowed to practise in England, that the State should provide the necessary funds for conveying both ,witneeses and lawyers, and political offences -were ex- chided, such a.s treason • felony, sedition, and seditious libel. The crimes that could be tried in England were murder, attempt to murder; aggravated crimes ,of vio- lence, arson, and razing and 'firing dwellings. In all eases the bill should only apply in districts proclaimed by the Lord Lieutenant, who would also have power to proclaim dangerous associations that disturbed • law or order. The proclamation of any association should 'he submitted to Parliament within 73411ren days, and if rarliament condemned it, the proclama- tion would have no force. The Government proposed that the Bill should not be limited in point of time. He concluded as follows :--For the first time in the history of this country., the victims of oppression, outrage, and murder--(Miessterial cheers)---have called upon the, Government of the country to protect them, and that Government has not been supported by . the English minority. That is no reason and should be no reason why we shall not do it alone. We sthould be utterly fail- ing in what I conceive to be the firstduty of a Govern- ment if, through any fear of parliamentary opposition, any dread of a hostile minority, we were to neglect or defer for one single day our answer to the appeal which cornea up to us from any part of disturbed Ireland. Many of those who are most devoted in the canee of liberty forget the respect due to the cause of order. will not ask whether these two great principles are or are not ever. opposed. For 700 wears they had hated each other; and if B't years after there- tended union the best thing that could be done was to suspend evory liberty in Ireland he should b iisposed to abandon public agitation, for be should coosider that man a slave who would submit to it. It was a good. thing for England, as well as for Ireland, that the Opposi- tion represented the majority of the English people..., Therecould but be one result of such a' measure—to dis- organise society and drive the people back to the horrors , of former years. A more miserable case on which to found a measure of coercion he never heard. , Three of the divisions of Mayo were as peaceable as Surrey or Sussex, and the only disorder in East Mayo was that the people there had upon his advice adopted the plan of campaign. The Chief Secretary bad sue- ceeded in proving nothing but his own ignorance of the country he sought to govern, and the ; sooner he quitted his present office the better it , would be both for Ireland and himself. The honourable member went at considerable length into the instances in which the plan of campaign had been resorted to for the purpose of justifying the course that had been taken, and afterwards examined with some minuteness the evidence taken before the Cowper Commission. He had, be said, advised Nationalists not to tender them- selves as witnesses, and their representatives did not acoept the statements in the Blue Book as a fair present- ment ef their case, but regarded the volume as a collec- tion of evidence packed in the interest of landlords. Irish landlords were defending not the union, but their own rack rents. Me next proceeded to discuss the ques- tion of land purchase, but The SPEAKER, interrupting him, pointed out that he was going wide of the mark in discussing land purchase on a bill for the amendment of the criminal law.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIMRSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shor ly after four o'clock.

TERRIBLE MURDER AT UR EWE. A shocking tragedy was committed in Henry-street, Church C,oppenhall, a suburb of Crewe, on Saturday, tinder circumstances which caused a great deal of excite- ment. A man named Henry Griffiths, his wife Sarah Griffiths, aged 59, and a niece named Mary Jones, aged nine years, in a cottage fit Henry-street, almost adjoining • tnitive Methodist Chapel. About eleven o'clock on day morning, the woman Sarah Griffiths was seen byte married sister (who lives in a house ad- joining) in, her garden, and she asked her to tell a man that she would•atot want any buttermilk that morning. The woman then vturned to her house. Shortly afterwards her niece, the little girl. Mary Jones, returned from the Co-operative Society with some goods, and also went into the house. The neigh- bours heard no struggle nor cries, but on Mrs. Griffiths' husband returning from his work about 12 15, he found his mile lying in a pool of blood in the kitchen, and her niece lying alongside, unconscious, and her face terribly disfigured. From the position .01 the dead body, it 'appeared that the woman must have been knocked down, and, the police believe, kicked about the head. There was a fatal wound behind the ear, which appears to have been indicted by a clog. A medical examination showed serious bruises-on the Wt side, and several ribs were broken. The woman appeared to have been jumped upon-after she had fallen. The little girl seems to have been attacked on her entering the house, as she was lying beside her aunt with her jacket on, and her hat near. The supposition is that the woman was attacked when alone in the house, and that the little girl returning unexpectedly, the murderer set upon her to prevent her giving an alarm. The tongs, and poker bore bleed stains, and seem to have been the instruments with which the blows were inflicted. One prong of the tongs was bent, which suggests the terrible force with which they must have been used. Large pools of blood covered the floor, and it. is most extraor- dinary that the deceased's neighbours heard nothing-of the occurrence until it was discovered by the husband on his return from Crewe Railway Works. The neigh- bourhood is most thickly populated. The house in which the deceased lived is well exposed back and front, and this, together with the fact that the crime was com- mitted at noonday, when hundreds of persons were up and down the streets, involves the affair in a great deal of mystery. It is said that three tramps were seen near the house during the morning, and the police were en- gaged all Saturday afternoon in visiting lodging-houses in the borough. On a further examination of the house the Police found a "dolly peg" with the head broken off, and this was besin:wtr with blood. It was found also that a drawer in which the deceased usually-kept money had been ransacked, and about 18s. stolen. Robbery, therefore seems to be the motive which prompted the crime. Late on Saturday evening- the little girl recovered consciousness, and made several statements which enabled the police to prosecute their inquiries. Imme- diately afterwards the police apprehended Thos. Henry 'Sevin, aged 21, a nephew of the deceased, and he was charged with the crime. Several tramps -have also been arrested in Cheshire and Staffordshire, on suspicion, but have since been discharged, and Sevin who on Mon- day offered to tell the magistrates "all about it," is under remand.

Mr. DILLON turned to Mr. Chamberlain's speech in April last, in which he advised the Prime Minister to continue the truce in Ireland, to suspend evictions for six months, and to leave the question of arrears to be dealt with afterwards, and wanted to know what had occurred since to cause the right honourable gentleman to change that view. It would be the duty of Irish members to resist this measure in every way that the rules of Parliament admitted of, and he believed they would be supported in that resistance by the entire body of the Liberal party, and by the people of England. (Cheers.) He should continue to carry on the plan of campaign in Ireland. He cared not whether he was tried in Dublin or at the Old Bailey, and if the Government succeeded in convicting him, on their heads be the crimes and horrors that might ensue. (Loud cheers.) • The honourable member, who ruse at 7 15, did not re- sume his seat until 10 40. Mr. HALDANE declared that they had before them a proposition of a character so extraordinary and of a stringency so remarkable that it almost took one's breath away. Lord LYASIDIGTON, as a Liberal Unionist, in offering the measure a general support, for he would not pledge him- self to details, rested his case not on the amount of . crime, but on the plain duty of supporting the only pos- sible Unionist Government in enforcing authority and securing to our Irish fellow subjects the protection of the laws of the British Parliament. The Unionist party I had never surrendered Imperial considerations to the t; argument of 'despair, and their duty was to prove that :1 the government of Ireland by England was not an ini- ; possibility. (Ministerial cheers.) He was sure the democracy of this country had no sympathy with out- ' rage, and that they regarded with indignation the con- spiracy to obstruct the business of the House of Com- mons, (Cries of'" Order.") , MR. HKALY : I have great respect for the noble Lord, but I wish to ask if lie is in order in speaking of a con- ; spiracy in this House 'for the purpose of obstructing business. •

The funeral of Sarah Griffiths took place on Wednesday afternoon. The streets were crowded all the way to the churchyard, a distance of nearly a mile. The deceased was connecred with the Primitive Methodist Chapel, which ad- joins her residence, and there were many members of the congregation in the procession. Thousands of persons were present at the cemetery, and much sympathy was shown for ths murdered woman's husband—an old man bordering on 70 years of age, who had to be supported at the grave side.—The little girl, Mary Jones, who was so dreadfully in- jured, is slowly recovering, and her condition on Wednesday was reported to be mach better. The police have taken her depositions, and these will form the chief evidence against her half brother, Thomas Bevin, who is in custody.

THE ALL-NIGHT SITTING.—VOTING BY CONARVATIVE MEMBERS WHO HAD PAIRED.—In reply to Mr. Broadhurst, Mr. Bars Tows said that ahhough paired for the night of the 21st inst., he had voted in three divisions after ten' o'clock on the morning of the 22nd, having been informed that, according to the rules of the House, he was entitled to do so.—Mr. Arnsom MORLEY then asked if it was true that 25 members on the Government side of the House, who were paired for the night of Monday, thei 21st, lad nevertheless voted in several divisions during the same sitting?—Lord R. CHURCHILL rose to order. There was no precedent for discussing without notice questions regarding the pairing of members, which was not a practise in any way recognised by the House,. which did not in its public capaeity take any cognisance of or record pairs.—The SPEAKER said that he thought it convenient to allow the question to be put, in order that the doubts that seemed to exist as to the proper practice to be pursued in a matter nearly affectioethe conduct of the business of the House might be set at west by some official statement -- Mr. AKERS DOUGLAS said that he believed that 25 Conser- vative members who paired for the night of the 21St did vote after 9 30 on the morning of the 22nd, inst. They did so with his. sanction, and he believed that they were justffiell in so doing because he had always understood that a pair entered into for the night only held good until the morning. If members desired to pair for the whole of a sitting the pair was so entered on the pair list. Be did not allow members who had paired for the night to vote in the closure division, or until after nine o'clock in the morning, when he con- sidered the pairs had lapsed, a view in which he was confirmed by the vice-presidentof the Council (a former \nip), by the leader of the House, by the member for the University of Oxford (Sir J. Mowbray), and by Mr. Sclaterßooth. He would suggest that those who were responsible for the organisation of parties in the House' should meet and settle a rule which would no doubt be accepted and acted on by all.—Mr. R. W. DUFF con-, tended that a pair for the night meant a pair for the whole sitting, and said that that was the impression of Lord Kensington, who had acted as whip for several years.—Mr. ARNOLD MORLEY said that he had only put' the question in order to obtain an understanding on the subject. div.head: IRISH LAND BILL.
div.p: IRISH LAND BILL.

Earl CADOGAN rose to call attention to recent legislation with reference to land in Ireland, and to present a bill. He I said that on the previous night Lord Haitington had ob- served that it might be wise for Parliament to abstain from pny attempt to deal now with the settlement of rents AS fixed by the Act of 1881, and with that opinion the Go. vernmeot entirely concurred. The Royal Commission re= commended that leaseholders should be admitted to the benefits of the Land Act. It was further the opinion of the Government that the time had arrived when a large mea- sure must be formulated for dealing with the question of purchase by tenants of their holdings, and to that they mainly looked for the settlement of the great questions which disturbed Ireland. It was proposed to deal with the land question in two parts. The bill he now introduced would deal with the urgent and difficult questions arising out of the Act of 1881, and also wito a large bill for purchase—in other words, a measure for the abolition of dual ownership created by the Act of 1881. The subjects now to be dealt with would be questions re- garding tenure, questions regarding appeals, and questions relating to equitable jurisdiction. The bill proposed that leaseholders &mild be included in the provisions of the Land Act. As to ejhtments, it was proposed that notice should be served by the landlord when he obtained a writ of ejectment from the court, and that when the tenant received the notice he should be ipso facto a caretaker, and the period of redemption would com- mence from that day. It was proposed that the middleman who had sublet his holding should in certain cases be able to surrender his tenancy. As to appeals, the Lord Lieu- tenant is to have power to constitute an Appeal Commission, and to associate with the ordinary members a Judge of the Supreme Court or some of the most -experienced of the CountytCourt Judges. On the question of equitable juris- diction it was proposed that, in bankruptcy proceedings, the County Court Judge, while granting to the landlord the judgment to which he was entitled, might put a reasonable delay on the execution of it; and, finally, the bill• would provide for the exemption of the landlord from the payment of rates if a tenant was in occupation and did not pay the rent.

Earl GRANVILLE suggested that it would be convenient if some member of the Government would offer a general statement as to what would be the character of the further legislation to be proposed. He pointed out that the bill contained no provision for the revision of rent, and corn- planed of the one-sided character of the meaeure.—Earl COWPER said the bill had a fatal objection, for in order to get a redaction of rent the tenant would have to compel the landlord to get a writ of ejectment. —After some re- marks from the Earl of Belmore and the Earl of Dunraven, the bill ,was read a Orst time, and the second reading was fixed for Thursday, the 21st of April. The Lord Chancellor presented a bill for facilitating the registration and transfer of land, and it was read .a first time. The House rose at 730.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Taukspei.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Taukspei.
The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. . .

TEE COBRCION BILL.—The debate on the Coercion Bill was resumed by Mr. LABODCEERE. Healing with the Judges' charges quoted by the Chief Secretary, he said those were excited harangues, delivered when there hap- pened to bee vacancy in the Court of Common Pleas. He declared that three/as ito exceptionalcrime in Ireland, and in regard to intimidation said there had been the grossest exaggeration. One object of the bill was to maintain unjust rents in order to carry afterwards some measure to enable landlords toeell their lancLat an unfair price, and the other object was to crush the Home Rule party.—Mr. GERALD BALEouR trusted the Government would persevere with their measure and pass it with all the expedition whichlthe forms of the House would admit.—The debate was con- tinued by Mr. Wayman, Mr. W. Redmond. M. H. S. King, Mr. B. Rowlands, Mr. H. Lawson, Mr. Campbell-Banner- man, and the Attorney General.:—Mr. PARNELL moved the adjournment of the debate.—Mr. SMITH assented, and said be would invite the House to-morrow to come to a decision on the main question.

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.
Mr. Jos. Arch has announced his intention of contest- ing North-West Norfolk, should his petition against Lord Henry Bentinck be successful.

Lord Randolph Churchill arrived in London on Sun- day from the Continent, after an absence of nearly two months. His lordship reached Charing Cross at 530 p.m., having come from Paris, via Folkestone and Boulogne, and looked much improved in health. A Rome telegram says the question of the treatment of the Irish priests excites much interest in clerical circles, but it is believed that the Vatican will exercise openly no influence. Lord Salisbury, in acknowledgment of a vote of confidence in the Crovernment from the Norwich Conser- vative working men, says :—" We are much gratified to resolve the assurances, for it lea time when lawlessness and rebellion are receiving a kind of support which in the history of political parties they have never received before."

I thought it 111,N jttile cCe uOvernment not to believe them. "Pot 'e did not believe I should live ki so °oud Opposition cheers)—when a 111 ding, so insulting, so exasperating,

so utterly in contrast with the whole of the lessons that Irish history teaches would have been submitted to a British House of Commons. (Oppo- sition cheers.) We need hardly say that it will be the duty of the Opposition to resist this ill-conceived and ill•starred Coercion Bill by every legitimate means in their power. It is bad in principle because it is founded upon a lie; the condi- tion of Ireland, taking the whole countryfinto account, and taking into account too the hardships which the people have endured, is not worse than it was some time ago. It is on the whole better; there is less evidence of serious crime ; and there are hopeful signs of a disposition on the part of the people to rely upon constitutional agitation as the best way out of the difficulties which beset the country. It is bad in policy, because it will inevitably result not in mending matters, but in heightening disorder, and in increasing crime. Shall the law then be set at defiance, it may be asked? Certainly not; let the law as it exists be brought fully into operation, as it was when Mr. JOHN MORLEY was Secretary for Ireland; but at the same time let an honest and resolute attempt be made to remedy evils which are admitted to exist; and we venture to say there will be less either of fracture or failure of the law than will be found under a Coercion Act. Coercion has failed in every one of the eighty-six years in which it has been tried; and that, too, when for a time it has been backed up by a majority of the representatives of England, and Scotland and Wales, and of Ireland her- self. It is not likely to succeed when it is denounced by the voice of Ireland, of Scot- land, and of Wales, and by a large portion of the people of England. It is a bad weapon which will break in the hands of those who use it and wound them; it is a creature con- ceived in sin and shapen in iniquity, and it were well if it were dead and could be buried without the hope of a resurrection.

THE Liberal Unionists seem to be having a good deal of their own way in Parliament, and "et they are far from happy. They have been clamouring for coercion, and a Coercion Bill is now before them ; they have developed ideas upon the Irish land question, and those ideas the Gov-rnment—having none of their own—have adopted; and yet, so far from being able to lift up their hearts and rejoice, they are restless, and irritable, if not wholly miserable. They have made pretty good use of the Press—Tory as well as Liberal—but that is not enongh ; so they have now come upon the scene with a journal of their own ---" The Liberal Unionist." The advance copy which has reached us may be described as a strong number, in that it includes amongst its contributors Lord HAR- TINGTON, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, and Mr. W. S. CAINE; but it cannot be said that it takes up a strong position. And how will it be when these new !eader writers have, say, after a year or two, got a-weary of the P.D.'s cry for " copy " ? But this is perhaps trying to look too far into the dim and distant future. Lord HARTINGTON'S contribution shows that he still stands were he did; but he does not, like some of his supporters, lose either his head or his temper. He perceives the diffi- culties of the situation; apd he is candid enough to admit that "we are confronted at the present moment by the unsolved problem of the condition of Ireland in a more acute form than that in which it has been presented to us in past times." His remedy is to "bring back the Liberal party to the faith of constitutional reform, to seek for practical remedies for acknowledged and proved grievances." Precisely; but what is constitutional reform? And what is a practical remedy? The Liberals think it is constitutional to alter the constitution so as to grant Home Rule to Ireland; and they think, too, that that is a practical solution of the Irish problem. Lord HARTINGTON can- not agree with this, and in this respect he is, curiously, at odds with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. who has again and again expressed himself in favour of the principle of Home Rule. It is true that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN did not ap- prove of Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rul,3 Bill ; but that is dead and gone; and, as there is nothing left but the principle, ordinary peo- ple are puzzled to know what the member for 1 West Birmingham is quarrelling about. He would surely be better employed in getting Lord HARTINGTON to accept the principle of Home Rule, instead of allowing his lordship to declaim against it as unconstitutional. Can it be possible that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN does not agree with Lord HARTINGTCN in anything, except in the determination to keep the Tories in office? It must not be forgotten that, while the Rupert of the Radi- cals showed himself disposed to fight Mr. GLADSTONE'S Irish Land Bill tooth and nail, the Rip Van Winkle amongst the Liberals declared that if Home Rule was adopted the Land Bill was absolutely necessary. No wonder that the Irish problem is unsolved. How is it possible for any progress to bf made when two men who are in the same boat cannot agree as to which way they should go? In the article furnished by Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN, it is stated that the policy of the Liberals, "whether they intend it or not, must lead to separation." The Liberals, however, say exactly the reverse; they plead that to grant Ireland the power to manage her own affairs would cement the Union: that it would make the Sister Isle a source of strength rather than of weakness to England. And they are entitled to go a little further ; they are entitled to ask Mr. CHAMBERLAIN to point out specifically. and in detail, how he makes it out- that Mr. GLADSTONE, as a Home Ruler, must be stigmatised as a Sepa- ratist, while the member for West Birming- ham, as a Home Ruler, should always be spoken of as a Liberal Unionist? He tells us that "no evidence has been forthcoming, or can be produced, to prove that Mr. GLADSTONE'S bills, or any similar measures, would be accepted as a final settlement." We deny this in foto ; and affirm that ample evi- dence has been given by the Irish leaders, and by the. Irish people, that 'they would willingly have accepted Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule Bill, and made the best of it. But supposing, for argument's sake, it be conceded that the Bill would not have satis- fied "the American agitators" or the Irish themselves, are we to be led by the nose to the conclusion that the only thing that could be satisfactory would be a bill based on Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S notions of Home Rule? If the half loaf which Mr. GLADSTONE is as- sumed to have offered, would not be regarded as "final," surely there is nobody out of Bir- mingham who thinks that Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN'S dry crust would be accepted as suffi- cient. We can understand Lord HARTING. TON; he is distinctly opposed to Home Rule; but we must confess that we cannot understand the politician who, while accept- ing the principle of Home Rule, .argues as if •a final settlement could be arrived at by offering a small Instead of a large instalment.
THE 1

Mr. CAINE, as the third of the trid;seems to ' have got beyond reasoning; he talks about Itaking the war into the enemy's camp, and by this he means the Liberal camp. This is the policy which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN adVo. cated when he spoke of having triangular duels in each constituency. It may come to this, but we hope not; and we would ask the Liberal Unionists to take thought for the morrow. If they do not mind what they are about, they will make the bed so hard that they will not be able to lie on it them- selves.

div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
- - - March went out singing as if it meant it— "Oh bother the flowers that bloom in the
spring."

Another priest (Father Ryan) has now been sent to gaol. It is reported that Sir Gilbert Greenall paid Sunday visits to certain priests during the election campaign of 1885 to ex- plain the policy of the Tory party. Is it too much to expect that he will now renew his calls and explain his explanation? It may be that the present policy is one of Conciliation; but it looks very much like Coercion.

It is said that in view of the revelations arising out of the inquiry of the Manchester Health Committee, some of the members when they attend church are heard to say with special emphasis—" We have done those things that we ought not to have done, and left undone those things we ought to have done, and there is no health in us ; " while ordinary ratepayers, with no less fervour, are led to exclaim—" Good Lord deliver us."

Mr. W. H. Smith announced in the House of Commons on Monday that the Government had decided to adhere to Tuesday as the public holiday for the celebration of the Queen's Jubilee. It would appear to be of no moment to those in authority that her Majesty enters on the 51St year of her reign on Monday the zoth of June. But we must not be hard upon the Government in this matter; it is not unusual for them to be a day after the fair.

The word Jubilee, like Macbeth's "Amen," will stick in the throat before the year is over. And what "ways and ways of celebrating it. At Latchford, on Monday, it was suggested that the rates should be re- duced. Why, oh, why was it not thought of at the Warrington meeting? It was in Wales, was it not? that the inhabitants de- cided on an enlargement of the cemetery; and it is in Wales, too, that it has been " resolved to celebrate the Queen's Jubilee by providing a new parish hearse." A brand new hearse—picture it, think of it, Jubilee man. It is nearly as good as the Government celebration—a brand new Coercion Bill.

"With four exceptions, all the dissentient Liberals will vote for the first reading of the Coercion Bill. The four exceptions are Mr. Winterbotham, Mr. T. R. Buchanan, Mr. Barclay, and Mr. Jesse Collings, the intimate friend of Mr. Chamberlain."—Daily P2per. What, Jesse leave Joseph? They'll call it
• .. A case of desertion. . Ah ! the bill must be bad which thus/gives us
First fruits of Coercion.

The "London Times," the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and other and smaller fry seem to think they are doing a very clever thing when they set about connecting Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Parnell, and Mr. Parnell with crime in Ireland. They have already forgotten that Lord Carnarvon, with Lord Salisbury's consent, was not only connected with Mr. Parnell, but had interviews with him. These Tories have ridiculously short memories ; but give them rope enough and they will hang themselves.

Superintendent James, of Carmarthen, lost his life the other day through taking a full dose of chloral, when the surgeon's instruc- tions were to take half a dose. It was a clear case of death from misadventure: but the jury have brought in a verdict of" Death by the visitation of God." Such a verdict is absurd at any time—it is a relic of heathenish ignorance; but in the present case it is not too much to say that it is blasphemous.

The epidemic of measles in Warrington is still spreading, There have been as many as 250 cases and 29 deaths in a fortnight. We mention the matter not by way of exciting alarm—the simple fact is sufficiently alarming —but in order to point to the necessity of suffering inhabitants acting on the injunctions which Dr. Gornall, the Medical Officer of Health, has given in the placard which he has issued. In a matter of this kind the road to salvation is through isolation.

Township meetings would "seem to be township farces. Mr. Hawkins,lthe assistant overseer of Latchford. told the ratepayers, on Monday, that " the appointment of overseers was in the hands of the magistrates entirely," and that "they had no power whatever to hold a meeting," He may be altogether right, but if he is there is something alto- gether wrong. The inhabitants are being fooled to the top of their bent. The time is long overdue for a County Government Bill that will ;make these crooked things straight.

At the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Mon- day, there was quite a tussle as to the ap- pointment of overseers for Frodsham Lord- ship. A crowded meeting of ratepayers had nominated Mr. J. H. Hargreaves in place of Mr. J. Percival, one of the old overseers. But the Bench disregarded the decision of the meeting, and re-appointed Mr. Percival. Lord Tollemache, who presided, said they could not turn out the old overseers without some reason. But there was a reason—the decision of the ratepayers was a reason. It is true it counts for nothing at present; a lord who is also a magistrate may, it seems, outweigh a whole township of ratepayers.

Mr. W. Morris, master of the Church Schools, Weston, put one foot in it when he objected to a private adventure school being established in the neighbourhood; and he has now got the other foot fast by a defence which is no defence at all. How can it be the business either of School Attendance Committee or its officers to ascertain if a Particular person has the "intention to evade the compulsory clauses of the Educa- tion Act ? " It is quite enough to have to deal with actual offences; it is ridiculous to talk about ascertaining " intentions." Mr. Morris. as a schoolmaster, would seem to be very much abroad.

COLLIERY FATALITY AT WITISTON.—On Friday, Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at Whiston on the body of John Kavanagh, collier. From the evidence of G. Barton, (manager of the Carr Colliery Com- pany) and others, it appears that the deceased was engaged down the pit on Sunday night clearing away after a shot, when a stone, four feet in length and four inches thick, fell upon him from the roof. A verdict of accidental death was rettumed.

He will guarantee that they are not to be equalled in the country for clearness. coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet "How to preserve,the sight " free on application —Advt.

HALTON BURIAL BOARD.—For the third year in MIME- , sion the Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar, has been unanimonsly appointed chairman of the Board. Winzaas GETS—The weekly meeting was held in the National School, on Thursday. Owing to the serious indis- position of the vicar the chair was occupied by the Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson. Devotional exercises were engaged in and the members sang sacred songs.

Sr. MICHAEL AND ALL ANGEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN.— Mr. T. Kakbam, contractor, has commenced the erection of the wall round this edifice, and sufficient money having been subscribtd to complete the nave, the 'church will doubtless_be opened for divine worship in about a month.

TEE WIDNES FREE DINNER MOVEMENT Was brought to a termination yesterday. Since the beginning of January between 200 and 300 dinners have been served to th• poorer school children each week, and the exertions of Mr. S. B. Stringer in organising and carrying out the work deserves reCogeition. NEW COPPER WORKS AT DITToN.—New life has been infused into the hitherto lethargic village of Bitten by the erection of the extensive works for the Broughton Copper Company. Its every direction.dilapidated houses are being renevated, and new rows erected for the anticipated influx of workpeople. WIDNES.— FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.—The interest which is being taken in the recently-opened reading-room does not abate, as is evidenced by ;he following figures, indicative of the number who visited it during the week ending Wednes- day. March 30th :—Thursday, 577; Friday, 530; Saturday, 1,024; Monday, 618; Tuesday, 516; Wednesday, 472. WESTON WESLEYAN BIBLE CLASS.—The final meeting of this class for the winter session has been held in the school- room at Weston. A substantial tea was provided, the tables being presided over by Mrs. Price, Miss Ford, Miss Hughes, Miss Smith, and Miss Dnnbebbin. After tea an enjoyable evening was spent. The following took part in the pro- gramme—Miss Smith, Miss Emily Griffiths, Mr. J. Cooper, Mr. John Ball, and Mr. Price, superintendent of the Sunday School. . Mr. Ford was re-elected president, and Mr. J. Ball secretary.

POPULAR CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—Another of the series of popular concerts was given in Bethesda schoolroom, on Tuesday evening, to a good audience. The principal vocalists were Miss Clara Mouldsdale and Miss Pierpoint, and both contributed s-veral songs in capital style. The character sketches and comic songs (aided hy musical skill) of Mr. Harry Collins gave the utmost pleasure. Mrs W. B. Kay was the accompanist. The Mill Brow Military Band during the evening performed several selections ad• mire bl v. APPOINTMENT OF OVERSEERS AT RLINCORN.—The Run- corn magistrates, on Monday, appointed the following over- seers :—Runcorn, Wm. Whittaker, W. Handley, Edwin Imison, and Samuel Taylor; Sutton, Wm. Lowe, and John Bets; Weston, Edwin Aaron, and Thomas Ford; Stockham, Richard Nickaon and Joseph Baguley ; Halton, Thomas Wright and Hugh Rowe; Clifton, Wm. Baker and Joseph Stokes; Aston-by• Sutton, Geo. Percival and Wm. Wilkin- son; Aston Grange, James Buckstone and Joseph N. Holli- day. The appointment of Henry Cha-lea Duprez, as assis- tant overseer of Norton, was sanctioned. The magistrates appointed an additional two overseers for Runcorn because of the growing importance of the town. HALTON AND THE QUEEN'S JUBlLES.—Varions meetings of the inhabitants have been held of late, in her Majesty's (Queen Victoria's) Court Leet room, to consider the most suitable way of commemorating the above. There was a good attendance at the last meeting. The Vicar presided, and expressed an earnest wish to see lamps to light up the village, inasmuch as the Queen was the Baron of Halton. A. Jubilee clock, too, to be placed in the church, was sug- gested. but it was the feeliag of the meeting that a substan- tial treat to the aged poor and children should be first pro- vided, and afterwards see what balance, if any, remained for the commencement of some other fund. A committee was appointed, Sir Richard Brook, Bart., being asked to accept its presidency, and the Vicar the treasurership. Col- lectors for each township and hamlet in the parish were selected.

RUNCORN UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCM COMMITTEE.— The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner presided over the monthly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, when the school attendance officers were re-appointed as follows : Thomas Riley, Frodeham district at £35 a year ; W. de Prez, Budworth district. £3O a year, and George Ward, Weston district, and Albert Woodier, Halton district, £lO a year each. The salary of the clerk (Mr. H. Linaker) was fixed at £35 for the past year.—A, long letter was read from William Morris, master of the Weston Church School, with regard to the private adventure school at Weston, about which some discussion arose at the last meeting. fie denied that Miss Fitton was a certificated mistress, and inquired where the middle class scholars were to come from.—On the motion of the Rev. J. Lockwood, seconded by the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, it was resolved that the letter lie on the table. .

FATAL ACCIDENT AT WESTON POINT. -- Mr. Clarke Aspinall, coroner of Liverpool, held an inquiry at the Dale street Police-buildings, on Tuesday, into the circumstances surrounding the death of John Dempsey, 46 years of age, who belonged to Arklow, and was the mate of the schooner Hannibal, which on that day was lying in the river waiting for calmer weather. It appeared that the deceased was on board the vessel, at Weston Point, near Runcorn, on the 23rd March, and the hold of the vessel was being prepared to receive a cargo of salt. The mate was reaching for a rope to which he intended to hook a basket, when he over- balanced himself, and fell to the bottom of the hold, a dis- tance of 12 feet. Two doctors attended him, and he was then sent down to the Liverpool Landing-stacm, and removed to the Northern Hospital, where he died on Sunday after- noon from the effect of fractured ribs. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

CONFIRMATION SERVICR AT RUNCORN.—Tbe Bishop of Chester (Dr. Stubbs) held a confirmation service on Wed- nesday afternoon at the Parish Church, Runcorn, when 91 candidates were presented to his lordship. The church was occupied by a large congregation, and great interest was manifested in the proceedings. The service was full choral. Amongst the clergy present were the Rave A Maitland Wood, M.A., vicar of Runcorn; W Preston, M.A., vicar of Holy Trinity, Runcorn; John Lockwood, vicar of Halton ; H B Blogg, M.A • vicar of Frodsham ; J Li Wileockson, 8.A., incumbent of Weston Point; W Bryant, 8.A., J D Ozanne. 8.A., G A Tindall, 8.A., curates of the Parish Church ; Rev William Fielding, 8.A.. curate of Aston ; and G Fisher, 8.A., curate of Holy frinity. The candidates were addressed by the Bishop both before and after the ceremony of the laying on of hands. Forty-four of the candidates belonged to the parish of Runcorn ; 16 to the Trinity parish ; 16 to Weston Point; 12 to Halton; two to Frodsham, and one to Aston. A RUNAWAY HORSE AT RTNCORN.—On Tuesday morning great excitement was caused in Church-street by the run- ning away of a horse belosging to Ralph Gibson. green- grocer. Ashridge-street. The horse, which was attached to a cart laden with vegetables, took fright in Arthridge-street, and rushed 0 a rapiel speed towards the ticket office at the Bridge, but swerving suddenly, the animal dashed into the door of the house occupied by Mr. George Burrows. The door and framework was smashed to matchwood, and one of the shafts made a great gap in the wall of the lobby. Back- ing out of the lobby, the horse went off at a WO speed along Church-street, and one of the shafts being broken, the cart swayed about in it most dangerous fashion, and threatened every moment to crash through the window of one of the numerous shops along the street. At the bottom of Alcock-street Mr. Walter Yarwood, son of Mr. S. Tar. wood, auctioneer, pluckily sprang at the horse's head, and although dragged for a considerable distance whilst in a perilous position, he succeeded in bringing the animal to a standstill In its career the cart collided with a lamp post, which was damaged.
RUNCORN' RIFLE CLIME—GOLD MEDAL COMPETITION. —The firet shoot of the season was held on Saturday,,posi-
- tion and ranges as for let stage Queen's Prize, 1886. There was a strong left front wind, very puffy and vari- able, which blfft,d the skill of the marksmen. The follow- ing were the scores:—

T A.A. Lieutenant A. Timmins Sergeant W. 111. Harvey • B9 Private Joseph D•olown 72 Celour.Bergeant J. Mort 72 Lieutenant T. B. Ashton Sergeant-Instr ,ctor Player 7l Lanee-Oorporal Cooper Quartermaster-Bergeant Hankinson 7O Corporal Joynson Private Joseph Marsh . 69 Private George Littlemore • Corporal Holt 6B Private P. DavPs 6B Private N. Tomlinson Private Joseph (lark Private H. Bickford SIMMS CROSS PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES. The annual sale of work in connection with this place of worship was commenced on Wednesday afternoon, and concluded on Thursday ni4ht. The proceeds were to be devoted towards liquidating a debt of £2OO, incurred in the erection of four class-rooms on one side of the chapel. The Rev J CAlvert announced the reccApt of the following sub- scriptions :—A. friend £2O, Mr T C Edwards Moss £3. Messrs Vickers and sons .£2. Mr T 8 Timmis £2, Messrs T Bolton and Sons £1 is, Mr F H Gossage £l, Mr E K Muspratt £l., Messrs Dennis and Co. £l, and Mr J Titchett (Warrington) £l. The ceremony of opening the •sale was gracefully performed by Mrs S White, of Runcorn, and the announcement that she had given a donation of £lO was received with loud applause. The stalls were presided over by Mesdames Calv-qt, Williams, Dale, Owens, Rollason, Hall, Sage, Lee' Hewson, Be Iford, 8 Upward, Jones, Web' ster, Crossley, Pinchers, Munslow. Wharton, Roon, and Bradshaw ; Misses Wiles, Winders, F Wiles, arld Crawford. The proceeds on Wednesday amounted to £52. A second opening ceremony was performed on Thursday by Mr J LI Lee, who contributed £5 to the lands.

THE PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR, RUNCORN.—The ' total amount realised by this bazaar was £l9O, which is considered a very satisfactory result. SACRED CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—To-morrow (Sunday) evening the Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa Choir will give a sacred concert in Runcorn Public Hall. Mr. P. Richardson, of Liverpool, will assist. LACEY•STREET BAND OF HOPE. WIPERS—The members of this society gave an entertainment in the school-room, on Mooday evening, to a good audience. A capital programme of songs, recitations, , was gone through. Mr. J. Hough- ton presided. JUBILEE BALL AT WIDNFS.—A ball to which the term "jubilee" was prefixed was held in the Baths Assembly Room, on Monday evening, and was attended with con- siderable success. Messrs. Grice and Woods were the pro- moters, and Mr. G. J. Kiddie acted as M.C. Mr. C. Powell's band supplied the music. ALLEGED ROBBERY AT RUNCORN —Before Capt. Hazle- burst, at Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, Joseph Williams, a labourer, was charged with having on Monday stolen Sc from the Greenway Vaults, occupied by John Cox- hill. Mr. Coxhill caught the prisoner in the act of taking money from the till, from which at least three florins had disappeared. The prisoner was remanded until to-day. SERVICH OF ONO AT FARNWORTII.—On Monday even- ing a service of song, entitled " Little Jamie," was given by the members of the Farnworth Wesleyan Band of Hope, in the chapel, Derby-road. Mr. J. J. Cook, of St. Helena, presided, and there was ai good attendance. The musical selections were well rendered, the solos being given in a highly creditable manner. The Rev. J. Bryant read the narrative. A RUNCORN FLATMAN DROWNED —Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at the Bridge Hotel, Widnes, on the body of Thomas Reeder, aged 29, of Holloway-road. Runcorn. The deceased was mate of the flat Willie, which was lying in West Bank Dock during the week end. On Saturday night the deceased was seen to leave the Swann Inn, Waterloo-road, by a man who described him AS in a half-drunken condition', and on Sun. day afternoon his dead body was taken from the West Bank Dock. A verdict of "Found dead " was returned. ROBBERY IT WlDNES.—Wilfrid Jannion, a labourer, was brought before Mr. Deacon, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, charged with having stolen from the shop of Messrs. Calvert Bros., Victoria-road, three pairs of stocking worth 3s 61. On Satnrday night the prisoner was seen to take the stockiegs frore off a hook at th shop door by Thos. Finn, an apprentice plumber. of 16, Wellington-street, and Wm. Barnes, plumber, of 13, Faulkner-street, Runcorn., Finn pursued and caught the prisoner, who gave up the stockings and was afterwards apprehended by P.C. Hot- brook.—The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. WATERLOO BRIDGE RUNCORN.—At length the scheme for the widening of this bridge and the improvement of its approaches thereto is beginning to assume a practical shape. It is proposed to erect a parapet on each side of the bridge, or abutments of stone, and to remove the sharp corners at the junction of Waterloo-road by carryiug the road over a perrtion of the land attached to the stables of the Bridgewater Navigation Company. The Board of Commissioners, it may • be pointeal out, have no power to spend public money in the alteration of the bridge, because it is the private property of the Navigation Company, and steps are being taken Co have the fabric of the bridge vested in the Commieeioners. When this is accomplished the scheme can be carried out. TRESPASSERS: ON THE RAILWAY NEAR RUNCORN. On Monday, at. the Runcorn Petty Sessions, George Hughes, Major Hughes, George Darlington. Henry Darlington, and William Darlington, young men, were charged with having on the 6th March unlawfully trespas- sed upon the London and North-Western Railway at Clif- ton in such a manner as to expose themselves to risk of danger. The defendants pleaded guilty. Mr. Preston, soli- citor to the London and North-Western Railway CompanY, appeared to prosecute P.C. Fryer said that on the 6th March he saw the five defendants walking on the line of the London and North-Western Bail way Company at Clifton. —Mr. Kenyon, stationmaster at Sutton Weaver, corrobora- ted.—Superintendent Hollingsworth said that men like the defendants did not only confine their trespass to the rail- way, but they did damage to fields by crossing them. A fine of 5s and its 6d costs in each case was imposed. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—At Widnes Petty Seesions, on Thursday, Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk to the Wid- nes School Board, prosecuted the following persons for not sending their children regularly to school :—Dennis Malone, Lawrence Kenny, John Clegg (two cases), Richard Traynor, and Michael McPa,rtland. The usual penalty of 55 was imposed in each case.—Mr. Denby applied that John Hilles, aged 10, should be sent to an industrial school. The boy was the son of the late Dr. Bilks. His mother bad married a labourer named George Rozelle, hut neither could control the boy. what did as he liked.—Mrs. Rozelle said she had taken the boy frequently to school, but he had run out again; and had stayed out at night —Mr. Gaskell, sen., said , the Bench could not burden the ratepayers with the cost of I the boy's maintenance and education. If necessary the parents must give him reasonable chastisement, and make him go to school. A fine of 5s would be imposed in the present instance. ' MARRIAGE OF MISS MCCLELLAN AT FARNWORTH.— The marriage of Miss McClellan, second daughter of the late Mr. John McClellan, chemical manufacturer, of Widnes, to Mr.. Gilbert R. Leah, Liscard, Cheshire, took place on Tuesday, at the Parish Church, Farnworth. The bridal party was entertained at Hiehfield House, Appleton, the residence of Mr. Alexander McClellan. Mr. Herbert Leah acted as best man, and the bride. who was attired in a hand- some dark green travelling dress with bonnet to match, was given away by her brother. The bridesmaids were Miss Katie Wall, Miss Gladys Brunner Miss Mary Newton, and Miss Millicent McClellan, the three latter of whom were attired in picturesque sailor costumes. Additional Interest was lent to the ceremony by the pretence of the choir, who rendered the usual marriage hymn as the bridal party entered the church. The Rev. Usher Beers Myles, MA., of Aekam Richard, York, was the officiating minister. The newly-married pair afterwards left Farnworth for London. The presents were about 100 in number. FATAL ACCIDENT AT RIINCORN.—On Thursday mornieg William Gerrard, 51 years of age, who formerly resided at 14, Heathcote-street, Tunnel-road, Edge Hill, died at the Northern Hospital, Liverpool, from injuries received on the previous day at the works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company. Gerrard was employed at the works as a fitter, and on Wednesday morning he was taking a "short cut" to the fitting shop, across a neutralising well. Being short- sighted, Gerrard apparently did not notice that the covering boards had been removed from the well to permit of its being cleaned, and he fell into the tank, which contained about fifteen inches of chloride of manganese liquor, heated to 140 degrees F. His cries for help quickly brought two men, who were working in the vicinity, to his aid, and they quickly rescued him from the hot liquid, but not before he had been severely scalded about the legs and lower parts of the body. He was at mace conveyed to the laboratory where bis injuries were dressed, and Dr. McDougall arriving soon afterwards, did all in his power to relieve the sufferer. At his own request Gerrard was conveyed to the Northern Hospital, Liverpool, where he died as stated through the shock to the system —An inquest wee held on the body, yesterday, by Mr. Clarke Aspinall, coroner of Liverpool, and a verdict of accidental death was returned. TOWNSHIP MEETING At WIDNES —The annual meeting of the Veetry of the inhabitants of Widnes was held in the Overseer's Office, Victoria-road, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. James White presided, and there were present Messrs. R. Fogg, F. H. Pankhurat. T. S. Swale, and J. Goff (assistant overseer).—The Chairman remarked that the presence of so few ratepayers showed the confidence they had in the overseers, and explained that the overseers com- menced the year with a deficit of £156, and in consequence of the reduction of 231 per cent in the manufacturers' assessments it was necessary to levy a rate of 2s 4d in the £ to meet the demands on the overseers. That rate had more than realised their expectations, and there was now a balance of £6OO to carry forward to next year. (Hear, hear.) The next thing they had to do was to estimate for the coming year. The School Board had issued a demand for £3,600, and the Union and County demand would be £8,600, which, with £2OO for other purposes. made a total of £12,400 required. A rate of 2s in the £ wauld realise £ll 904 ; and adding to that sum the balance of MOO gave £12,501. this indicating a small balance after meeting all calls. Mr. White spoke in high terms of praise of the able and efficient services of Mr. Goff, and axpressed a wish that. having been an overseer for three years, another gentleman should be nominated to fill his (Mr. White's) place.—lt was unanimously resolved to submit the names of the following gentlemen to the magistrates :—Jeanes White, J. Midwood, R. Fogg, S. Robinson, S. B. Stringer, F. Neil, S. Owens, F. H. Pankhurst, and W. Sadler—ln answer to a question, Mr. White said the 23 rate would be made up of 7d for School Board, 5d for the County, and is for the Union. CHARGE AGAINST A WESTERN PUBLICAN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Benedict B. Burchall, landlord of the Royal Oak publlchouse, Weston, was charged with selling intoxicating liquors to a drunken won named Thomas Keogh, and also with unlawfully permitting drun- kenness on his premises. Mr. F. A. Lake defended. P.C. Breeze deposed that on the 22nd March he visited the Royal Oak Inn accompanied by P.C. Fryer. In the taproom they found Keogh drunk and fast asleep. On the table near him Was a pint pet containing beer.—ln reply to Mr. Lake, P.C. Fryer said Keogh never got up and never spoke. His head was between his legs. (Laughter.) The landlord said the beer belonged to another person who had just gone out.— Re-examined by Superintendent Hollingworth, Fryer said they had watched the house ten minutes and no person had left it—Mr. Lake said Keogh, who had been at work all the night previous, had gone into the house, and being tired and I exhausted he had fallen into a doze. When the officers matered they found him in that condition, and he contended that there was no evidence to show that he was drank. The officers made no examination of the the man, and it was one of the most ridiculous things he bad ever met with to charge a mars with being drunk because he did not stand up and talk clearly after a sound sleep on being confronted by two offers—Keogh supported this statement on oath, and John Kelly, chemical labourer, stated that Keogh was perfectly sober. Three of them had two pints each.—Asked by Mr. Lake how many pints would make a man drink, witness said he could driek ten or twelve pints, and would not be drunk. (Loud laughter.) Two pints wonld not cure a man's thirst. (Renewed laughter.) —A number of other witnesses having deposed to Keogh's sobriety, the Bench dismissed the charge of stlol3ls'ing drink to a drunken person on the ground that it was not proved, but for permitting drunkenness Burchall was tined lOs and costs 19e61, and Keogh, for being drunk, was fined 53 tied costs 12s 63,
n I WIDNES SCTIOOL FEE QUESTION.—We understand that the Education Department have sanctioned the scale of increased fees for the Widnes Board Schools.

',Beeman AT Romoax.—To a good audience at the Na- tional School, o c Thursday evening, the Rev. W. Bryant, citrate, delivered a lecture on "Oxygen and hydrogen," illustrated by experimente: THE WIDNES HALF-HOLIDAY MOvEMENT.—With the exception of the grocers, the tradesmen of Widnee have for several years past enjoyed a half-holiday on each Thurs- (ley, and now the grocers, mainly through the exertions of Mr. William Farrant, of Waterloo-road, have also decided to close their establishments on the afternoon of that day. Fifty-three grocers have signed an agreement to that effect. RUNCORN INDUSTRIAL BUILDING BOCIETY.—The fourth appropriation meeting of this society was held in the class- room, National School. on 1 uesday evening, the ream being well filled. Mr. Albert Jordan was voted to the chair. The secretary offered £lOO share for sale. £lO was at once tendered for the same, and after some brisk bidding the share was at length knocked down to Mr. George T. Wain- wright. a well-known member of the Runcorn Football Club, for the sum of £3l 10a. Mr. Wainwright having two shares in his hook, was accordingly declared to be en- titled loan advance of £2OO, free of interest, for which he had to papa premium of £63. A vote of thanks to the chairman terminated the proceedines. BRUTALITY TO A HORSE AT RUNCORN.--9t Runcorn ! Petty Sessions on Monday, William Martin, a flatman, liv- ing at the Brick-kiln housee, Canal-bank. was charged with cruelly illtreating a horse by kicking and beating it.—P.C. Millington said that on Saturday, the 12th March, he wee Proceeding behind the defendant's flat along the Bridge- water Canal for upwards of half a mile. In that dietetics the defendant kicked the horse several times on the fore ' legs and in the stomach. He was wearing clogs at the time. He then beat the horse unmercifully with a rope, when witness went to him and told him that he sheuld re- port the case.—The prisoner's excuse was that the horse had run away, and that he only kicked it with the side of his foot when in a paspiou.—The defendant was fined lOs and 9s 6d costa. ALLEGED THEFT OF A FOOTBALL —On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Samuel Fenny. 17 years of age, of , Farnworth, was charged with stealing a football, value ; 3s 6d, the property of Robert Lowe, of Rainhill. The corn- plainant said he purchased the ball for his eon, aged four, ' and he last saw it nn Saturday. It was taken on Mondav, and be traced it to the prisoner's house. When apprehended by P.C. Heaton, the prisoner said be saw some boys playing with the ball atßainhill, and as it was burst he offered them a penny for it, but they told him it was no good and they ; gave it to him.—Mr. Swift defended and contended that there was no evidence to show that the ball was stolen, and argued that the boy's story, which he had consistently maintained, was true. He called the prisoner's grandfather John Abbott, cucumber grower, Farnworth. who said the boys from whom the prisoner got the ball were from 710 14 years of age.—The Bench dismissed the case. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. R. Gasket], menr., and Mr. G. Pilkington, John Slater' a rough- looking labourer, was charged with committing a breach of the peace, and also with assaulting Constables McGinie and Strong. The constables were on duty in Ann-street at eleven o'clock on Tuesday night, when the prisoner's father and- mother complained that he had threatened to kill his sister during the night. His parents and sister were afraid to enter the house, but whilst the officers were present, the sister ventured to do so, whereupon the pri- soner struck her twice. The officers seized hide and he threw himself to the ground and kicked McGinis twice on the forehead. He also kicked Strong on the face, and, in the words of that officer, acted like a madman.—The pri- soner pleaded gully to all the charges and said his only excuse was that be was drunk.—lnspector Wood mentioned that the prisoner had been eleven times before the Bench ; and Mr. Gaskell said the police were exposed very much to danger in discharge of their duty, and it was the duty Of the magistrates to protect them and visit with severity any violence shown towarda them. The prisoner was sen- tenced to two months' hard labour for the assaults. The , Charge of committing a breach of the peace was withdrawn, oaths suggestion of the Bench.
