Contests will take place at Weston and Lower Walton, but it is generally thought that the sitting members will retain their seats. FOOTBALL—Runcorn v. Mr. T. B Sutton's Tenet: On Wednesday Mr. T. R. Sutton opposed Rnncorn with his famous Lancastrian team, the match being in aid of the band fund of the 2nd Cheshire Rifle Volunteers, whose services are gratditously rendered to the Runcorn Club throughout the season. The event excited an extraordinary amount of interest in the district, and as business was sus- pended at an eerlv hour of the day, AD unusually large and enthusiastic crowd visited the enclosure at Irwell-lane, fully 6,000 persons being present. Kemble kicked off, and from Wood's return the hall rolled into touch, and a dead ball fell to the visiting team. Some good passing by the home threerenarters at length enabled Cawley to locate the play in mid-field, from whence H. Hughes ran grandly to the 25 line. Here a stout scrimmage was waged, and a moment later Clark crossed the visitors' line amidst tumul- tons applanse. Barnes failed to enhance the point. When the interval was Announced, Runcorn was leading by a try, the minor points being equal in number. The play in the second half became exceedingly fast, and Barnes led a movement, but although he received no sup- port, the advantage was maintained. Coop now evoked the enthusiasm of the sympathetic crowd, and having taken the play to the Runcorn line, Spencer crossed over, when Coop landed a goal amid renewed applanse. Play had no sooner been resumed from ties centre than W Hughes ran in on the extreme left, hat without the value of the point being en- banned, although a good effort wits made. Eventually a splendidly-coatested game ended in favour of Mr Sutton's team by a goal and four minor; to two tries and four minors. LANCASHIRE ANNUAL SESSION.—On Thursday morning the annual session of the peace for Lanca-. shire was held at the County 11411,Preston. A num- ber of pensions and gratuities were passed, and several notices of motion were on the agenda for Iconsideration. These include a proposal that a sum of .£17,000 be raised in connection with the County Lunatic Asylum at Rainhill for the comple- tion of the sewage" farm, the rain water reservoir, the formation of roads, and other works. THE MANCItIIItTICE HEALTH COMMITTEE'S IN- Qtirnir.—A sensation was caused by some extraor- dinary evidence in the Manchester Health Com- mittee inquiry on Tuesday. Mr. Thomas Bright swore that when he was chairman of the Baths Committee, Alderman Brown offered him a bribe of £lOO to influence the committee to purchase land in which Brown was interested. Mr. Brown entered the box, and swore that he never offered such a bribe ;. but that Mr. Bright gave him £3 for nego- tiating a purchase of property in a private transac- tion. Mr. Greaves, elective auditor, gave evidence that Brown told him that he offered Bright the £lOO, and led him to believe' that Bright had done better in another quarter. Mr. Bright, re-called, declared that he never received a penny from any- one during his connection with the Corporation. Other members of the Council testified that Bright told them of the offer at the time. THE LIVERPOOL JUBILEE EXHIBITION.—At the weekly meeting of the Executive Council of the Liverpool Jubilee Exhibition, held on Tuesday, Sir David Radcliffe presiding, the following gentlemen were present :—Messrs. J. S. Harmood Banner, W. Bennett, H. Cookson, William Croslield, J. Eshelby, I. H. E. Gill, John Moulding, F. J. Leslie, Richard Ripley, W. .T. Winstanley, and J. F. Doyle.. The minutes of the various committees were considered, and amongst the matters of public interest may be mentioned the decision of the council to construct illuminated fountains. A large number of pictures. mainly illustrative of the wars during the reign of her Majesty, have been secured, and the negocia- tions with local theatrical managers have been settled on a satisfactory basis, so that dramatic per- formances will be added to the other numerous at- tractiOns to be offered to the public. It was decided to allow exhibitors to sell any article manufactured in the machinery court if not in the nature of refreshments. The council also- sanctioned the ar- rangement of the Liverpool courts in the Queen Anne style, as recommended by the committee. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday at Hutto!? Workhouse, Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present the Revs J W N Tanner, J Lockwood, T Whitley, Mews J Weir, Lewis, Stokes, Hadfield, Brandreth, W Whitlow, Wallington, Pair, Aaron, Hamilton, Davies, and H Linaker (Clerk).

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER.
div.p: THE MEDICAL OFFICER.

The Rev. J. Lockwood moved the re-appointment of Dr. Adams as medics! officer of health, at the usual salary of £l2O a year. He 111,49 cure they were all satisfied with the work Dr. Adams had done, and with the manner in which he had done it.—Mr. Hadfield seconded the motion.—Mr. Parr thought the odd £2O so mach money thrown awaf.—The Clerk remarked that the Local Government Board paid half of the salary, and that Beard would not sanction a lower amount.—Mr. Parr moved that the salary be reduced to £loo.—The Rev. J. Lockwood said Dr. Adams had held the appointment for four years. and he would not accept less than the sum he had received annually.—Mr. Parr said someone else perhaps would.—Mr. Whitlow seconded Mr. Parr's amendment, for which only four members voted, and the remainder for the original proposition, which was de- clared carried.

THE CLERICS SALARY. The Clerk said he hid had extra work during the past year in connection with the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, but he was willing to accept the usual sum of £B5 for his past yetr's services—Mr. Parr moved a resolution fixing the salary at that amount, and it was carried unanimously.

DIPTHERTA. Dr. Adams reported an outbreak of diptheria at a cottage at Aston Heath. The patient iv 4.3 a girl nine years of age, and there was no doubt the disease bad arisen.tbrough the damp condition of the house. He suggested that a. foundation drain should be laid.—The report was adopted FRODSHAM WATER SCHEAM

The Chairman explained that the Frodshatn Parochial Committee recommended that the Clerk make a journey to London to confer with the Local Government Board with regard to a water supply for Frodsham, and also as to the repayment of the money already spent in endeavouring to provide a scheme. Several letters had been received from the Local Government Board, but they were not of a char- acter satisfactory to the Committee, who considered that the best plan was to have a personal interview. The sum of £l,OOO had been expended upon the water scheme, £4OO of which the Board stated must be repaid in 30 years; £475 in 5 years, and the remaining £175 at once.—The Clerk re- marked that if the money had to be repaid in this manner it would mean a Iti,avv rate of about 6J in the pound for Frodsbarn.—ln reply to Mr. Whitlow, the Chairman said the Committee had obtained water arlo'ch they considerad sufficient in quantity and pure in quality, but the Local Government Board, would not sanction the scheme. Mr. Whitlow asked if they could not get water from the Liver- pool Water Mains.—The Clerk said he had on behalf of the late Marquis of Cholmondeky made an arrangement for water to be supplied at 9d per 1,000 gallons. At Frodsham they wanted 30,000 gallons per day, which would mean 25a per day. Then the Liverpool water mains did not come within 4 miles of Frodshitm, and altogether this would be a very expensive mode of getting water.—Mr. Aaron moved that the Committee's recommendation be adopted. The job had been on the carpet long enough, and if it rested with the Local Government Board nothing would ever be done. That Board was composed of nothing but a lot of "was- trail "—a lot of pensioners that had to be kept some way or another.—Mr. Whitlow: The reporters had better not put that in or else you will get nothing. Mr. Aaron: They can pat it down I don't care the toss of a button for them. —Mr. Hadfield seconded the motion which was carried.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting, held at the Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present—the Revs. .1. W. N Tanner, J. Lockwood, and T. Whitley: Messrs. J. Weir, P. Speakman, E. Aaron, S. Taylor, J. Stokes, Warburton, Parr, Lewis. Smith, Hadfield, W. Whit- low, Kirkham, Davies, Brandreth, Foster, Pickering, Hamil- ton, Hewitt, Campkin, and H. Linaker (clerk).

div.head: THEI LUNATICS.
div.p: THEI LUNATICS.

The Clerk read a letter from the clerk to the Visiting Justices of the County Asylum, informing the Board that the charge for maintenance had been reduced to as 5d per head per week, commencing from the Ist January last.— Mr. Aaron: That is very low.—The Clerk : Yes. It was 7s 9d before for pauper lunatics. It now costs you less than it would in this house, because you get 4s per head back from Government. MR. WEIR AND THE LATE MATRON'S ALLOWANCE.

The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning an annual superannuation allowance of £3O to Mrs. Jones, the late matron of the Workhouse.—Mr. Weir said he had been one amongst others in supporting the granting of. thia allowance, and he thought it very proper. For the part he had takes, however, he was to be "kicked oat " of the guardianship of Lower Walton at this election. (" No, no.") He did not care whether he was elected or not ; he had done his duty conscientiously. A better matron than Mrs Jones they could not have, and he was happy to see that the Local Government Board had reported so favour- ably.—Mr. P. Speakman said he was glad the members had an opportunity of expresqinz their thanks to the Local Government Board for taeir noble conduct to Mrs. Jones, who was now a widow. It fall to the lot of few unions to have a better matron than Mrs Jone, to look after the affairs of the workhouse. (hoar, hear.) lie was very glad that their vice-chairman (Mr. Weir) had thepleasure of supporting so noble a cause ; and as for him being turned our, he did not think that would come to pass, and he was sure they would all be very sorry to lose Mr. Weir. The contest that was being breed on at Lower Walton would cost more he ventured to say than the ratepayers of that township would have to contribute towards Mrs Jones' sup- port in two or three generations. It looked more like pique than a question of the ratepayers interest. (Hear, hear.) It would be futile, he thought, to try and turn Mr. Weir out of the position which he had held for so long a period, and his opponents would be beaten with their own weapons. (Hear, hear.) He had great pleasure in speaking to the very great ability with which Mrs Jones managed the affairs of that union. (Applause).

div.head: ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended that the clerk's (Mr. H. Linaker's) salary for the past year be fixed at the usual earn of £B5, and that he also 19e allowed £35 for extra ser- vices a long list of which was read.—Mr Aar n moved, and Mr Lewis seconded, the adoption of the recommendation.— In reply to Mr Warburton, the Clerk said the present assessment of the Mersey Salt and Brine Company was about £1,400. The works, however, were not yet in full operation, but whea they were they would contribute from £2OO to £350 a year to the Urtion.—The motion was passed.

div.p: THE ELBCTION. The remuneration of the returning officer at the approach. ing election was fixed at £2O.
THE TENDERS.

A committee was appointed to consider the tenders, and the following were unanimously occepted, on the motion of the Rev J W N Tanner, seconded by Mr Speakman :—M ilk, Samuel Basnett Newton; COAL W and I Richardson, War- rington: cartage, William Grounds, Aston; meat. W Gill, Warrington • potatoes, William Tickle, Keckwick ; coffins, William Lightfoot, Dutton; beer and port wine, Thomas Price, Runcorn; groceries, Joseph Kidd, Frodstiam ; and drugs, I Speakman, Runcorn. The consideration of the tenders for boots and shoes and drapery was postponed until the next meeting. This was all the business.
A WIDNES PUBLICAN FINED.

James Taylor, landlord of the Angel and Elephant Inn, Appleton, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, to answer a charge of having, on Wednesday, the 9th March, permitted drunkenness to take place on his premises, and also with selling intoxicating liquors to a drunken person named Walter Wilson.—Mr. J. 0. Swift defended. • P.C. Almond deposed that at ten minutes past four on the day in question he went into the defendant's house, and in the taproom he saw five or six nayvies, all under the influence of drink. lie then went into the bar parlour, where he found Walter Wilson in a very drunken state_ He was sitting in a chair with a glass containing whisky on a table before him. He drew the attention of the landlord and his wife to Wilson's state, and told him he should have to take him to the police station. The land- lord, who was also under the influence of drink followed them into the street, and shouted at him (Almond).—ln answer to Mr. Swift, witness said Mr. Johnson, of St Helens told him that a man who ought to have been sell- ing eggs for him was drunk in Taylors. Mr. Johnson wanted to give him in charge for embezzlement, but witness informed him that he could not do so without a warrant. Mr. Johnson said the man was £3 5s deficient. —Police- Clerk Steele deposed that Wilson was very drunk at the police station, aud was unable to stand without assistance. —lnspector Wood also gave evidence as to Wilson's drunken condition.—Mr. Swift, for the defence, explained that Wil- son was in the employ of Mr. Johnson, grocer, of St. Helena. and on the afternoon in question a man bad come from St. Helens to take charge of the horse and cart and the eggs which Wilson had in his Custody; and it was because of a dispute between Wilson and young Johnson about money that the officer was called away from his fire- side. Almond saw Wilson outside the pealic-house, and had a long discussion with him in the highway twenty minutes previous to finding him in the public-house. He then took no notice of Wilson's drunken condition, and never threatened to lock him up on a charge of being drunk, and there could not have been so great a difference between his state then, and his condition twenty minutes afterwards. The fact was that Wilson was very ill, and had been unable to do his work on Monday and Tuesday, and after going round on Wednesday morning he was obliged to give up at noon. He was placed in an arm chair near the fire in order to wait for Mr. Johnson's arrival, and had only, during the time he was present, two pennyworth of whisky. When Mr. Vincent Johnson arrived, there was to dispute about Is lOid between him and Wilson, and Mr. Johnson perfectlythe influence of sober. It was untrue Improperly threatened to have Wilson locked up.—The de- fendant was called and gave evidence as to the illness of thha Wilson,atrbl Charles (defendant) f Bell, e ns porkadi ad n t 13) butcher, wagwase under Ann-stre drink.— et, Michael Barber, draper, Wigan, Mrs Taylor, and Thomas Mark, all deposed • that Wilson was perfectly sober, and Robert Newton, work- ing carpenter, stated that Wilson was very ill on Monday and Tuesday.—The Bench imposed a fine of 208 and costa I for permitting drunkenness; the other charge was with. . drawn.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

Royal Marines, was remanded to await an escort. MONDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) Alder- man Harrison, and Councillors Greening and Francomb. RETURNING FROII AINTREE.—WiIIiam McLaren, who said that he belonged to Manchester, was brought up on a , charge of having travelled from Aintree to War- rington, on the Cheshire Lines Railway, on Saturday, with- out having paid his fare with intent to defraud the com- pany.—Prisoner, who had neither money nor ticket in his v possession, was found underneath the seat of a carriage on u 4. the arrival of a train at Warrington Central Station on Saturday evening. A Cass OF EDSPICION.—Richard Jefferson, a rough-look- ing young man, was charged ith having been found on the premises of William Bradbury, Hoyle-street. with intent to commit a felony. Prisoner went into the scallery of Brad- bury's house, shutting the door after him, and when ob- served said that he had come to beg some bread. DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TMESDAY.—Beforer Messrs. E. Greenell, W. Long, J. C. Parr, W. C. Jones, E. Matson, and J. Neild, and Major Fox. Canxigss Dairneo.—Arthur Frith, a youth, was fined le and costs for riding on a cart without reins: and his brother. Oswald Frith, was fined in a like amount for a eimilar offence at Dutton. John Morgan, a young man, was also fined Is and costs. DRUNKENNESS.—John Doyle was fined 50 and costs for being drunk and disorderly at Grappenhall on the 15th March. DOG Cans: -A lizavY FlNE.—Jamee Buckley was charged with having refused to produce his dog license at the request of a policeman at Sevenoaks on the 28th Febru- ary. Defendant pleaded guilty, and said he refused to show the license because the officer spoke to him in such a commanding manner. The Chairman said it was the duty of men like the defendant to afford every facility to the police in the discharge of their duties. They would impose the full tine of £5 including costs. Defendant asked if he could appeal, ant the Clerk (Mr. Nicholson) said he might obtain that information for himself. At the close of the business Superintendent Hollinvworth asked for a distress warrant to be levied on Mr. Buckley's goeds, as that gen- tleman had said he would not pay the fine. Mr. Buckley said he did not decline to pay, but he thought the sentence was a shameful legal outrage. He asked if the Bench would not re-consider their decision. The Chairman said they would certiiely not. He did not understand whether or not Mr. Buckley declined to pay or not. Mr. Buck- ley: Ido not ay that ; can I appeal? COCHHEDGE MISSION BTAR OF HOPI V. BEDFORD.—These teams met for the second time this season at Warrington, on Saturday, when the game ended ia a draw, the score being —Star of Hope, 6 minors; Bedford, 2 minors.

WARRINGTON WANDERERS V. BEV7SET ROVERS. - This match was played on the ground of the latter and resulted in a victory for the visitors :—Wanderers, 1 goal, 1 try, 5 miners, and a disputed goal, to Rovers, 1 disputed frY• and 3 minors.

_ FRODSHAM V. Rutecome CAMDEN. This match was played at Frodsham on Saturday. RUNCORN 2ND TEAK V. NEW BRIGHTON OLYMTIC.—This match WAS played at Runcorn before a good number of spec- tators, and after a splendid and well-contested game victory rested with the borne team by two tries and three minor Points, to the Olympic three minors. Teams r—Runcorn— J Bowyer. back; T Whinvates, A Clare, and E Lunt, three- quarter backs; J Clare aud G WbiLby, half backs; .1 Gittens (captain), P Riley, E Andrews, T Abrams, T Cox A Raffe, F Hancock, W Jones, and R Dolan, forwards. WIDIVES T. WALICDEN —ln the presence of about 1,000 spectators. these team met on the Widnes ground on Sat- urday. Harding, Parkinson, Pervin, and Ridvard were ab- sent from the Widnes ranks. During the first half the visitors had the advantage of the wind and the slope, and pressed Widnes • freqnently, adding three dead balls and a touchdown before half-time. Immediately after the change of ends they succeeded in scoring another dead ball ; but that was all they were te obtain, Widnes having the subsequent play strongly in their favour. Smith came away with a fine dribble from the centre to the Walkden quarter, whence Howard ran to the line, where he was tackled and passed, and Hardman secured a try in the melee. Morris failed at the place. Widnes added a couple of minors, and then Farrell followed well after a kick by S. Binalearn, and when close on the visitors' line caught , the ball from Price's foot, and ran in and obtained a try. Kiddie took the place, but nothing resulted. Widnes com- pelled their opponents to save soon after, and the game closed with the score—Widnes, two tries and three minors ; Walkden, five miners. Teams: Widnes—S Bingham, back; Plumpton, Farrell, and Pennington, three-quarter backs; Howard and Fogg, half backs; Kiddie (captain), Smith, Corns, Meagher, Hard:ran, Woods, J Bingham, Hughes, and Morris, forwards. Walkden—Price, back ; Beon, Mar- tincroft, and Grundy. three-quarter backs • Cook and Wilcock, half backs; Rushton. Hindley, Reaves, Pres- cr.t, Gardner, G Jones, Evans, Walker, and Urmston, for- wards. RUNCORN T. ROCIIDALE ST. CLEMENTS.—This match was played at Rochdale on Saturday, being the first time of meeting this season. A large number of spectators lined the ropes when the teams appeared, Runcorn being represented by J Brazendale, back; W Riley, H C Speakman, and T Davies, three-quarter backs; H Hughes and H G Andrews, half backs; W Wright, W Hughes, W H Broady, W Faulk- ner, J Lewis, J Clark, G Wainwright, J Gatley, and J Barns, forwards. St. Clement's: Peel, back: Shepherd, Rig, and Collinae. three-quarter backs; Kenyon and Richardson. half backs; Dux, Oddy, Waugh, Holt, Mc- Hugh. Rtmsey, Pratt, Ridaugh, and Whitehead. forwards. Richardson, the home captain, winning the spin, chosti to play with the wind and hill in his favour, the wind at the time blowing strongly. Broady kicked off, aud the ball being charged down Davies was first to move, but St. Cle- ments soon extracted a minor point. Shepherd returned the kick out, when Speakman threw to Davies. but nothing was gained, Shepherd collaring. Clarke and Wainwricht made headway to centre, and Andrews kicking across the ground Riley made a strong effort to get in, and Collinge and Peel had to use their best endeavours to stop the raid. After some share scrimmaging on the home line Wright came through, Shepherd just dropping on the ball before him. conceding a touchdown. The game was contested in the Runcorn half for a time, a punt by Brazendale going into touch in goal. Play being resumed scrimmage after scrim- mage was formed, the home team endeavouring the whole of the game to keep the ball as tight in the packs as possi- ble, making the forward play very hard and monotonous. Davies ran out of his 25 and kicked well down the field, and Andrews ran from the subsequent scrimmage and threw to Speakman, who gave Riley a chance, but Callinge and Rigg spoiled and th• ball was driven back. Brazendale re- turned the ball. Richardson exchanged to Shepherd, who kicked well. A free kick fell to Speakman, but nothing re- sulted, and some passing was indulged in by Barns, Hughes, and Speakman, which ant the ball to the home quarter, where Speakman had a shot at goal, but the ball just passed

outside the posts. Another minor point was conceded to the home team by Peel, and ends were changed without a major point being scored. Rigg etarted the second half, and Lewis made a good return, and kicks were exchanged by 1 Davies and Peel, when play was brought about in the home quarter by Speakman, the ball going over the line dead. Scrimmage after scrimmage was formed in the St. Clement's quarter, and Andrews making a fine effort was held on the line, but grounded the ball. The referee, however, decided against him, and the St. Clements touched down. A drib- ble by Wright was checked close to the line by Rigg, and the home team having changed their tactics and played four ' three-quarters, frustrated some good efforts on the part of the visitors. Andrews, however, made another dart from the pack, and landed safely over, Broady's kick at goal failing. Following this, another dead ball was forced, and a hard-fought game, but not at all an interesting one, was , decided in favour of Runcorn by one try and five minors to four minors. _

WARRINGTON " A " Twit v. ARDWICZ ler.—These teams met at Warrington on Saturday. Henderson kicked off for Ar Iwick, and through the visiting forwards getting eff side a scrimmage was formed in centre. The home players, headed by Hackett and Thorn ley, brdke away, tak- ing play to the visitors' quarters, and Unsworth and Bate worked the ball to the line, but Morris afforded relief by a short kick into touch. Bate here retired owieg to an injury to his shoulder, Unsworth taking his place at half back. Whittle got hold and passed to Belshaw, who transferred to Boardman. This player put in a good kick, and Crum following up gained a try, Barnes kicking a goal. Bender- sod kicked off, and Molyneaux charging the ball down a scrimmage was formed in centre. Craghan, Molyneaux, and Adamson were now prominent, taking play to the visitors' territory, where Whittle passed to Barnes, who gained ground and got into a good kick. Hall returned well. Some good passing between Whittle, Belslaaw, and Boardman took place, the latter player kicking at goal, the ball being scrimmaged under the posts. Ardwick played a good defensive game, and the ball was worked back into touch near centre. Unsworth got possession from the line out, and made a short rum, theta Whittle passed to Belshaw, who repassed to Boardman. ibis player kicked to Hall, who was allowed a free kick for offside collaring. Whittle threw to Belthaw, who almost got over, being stooped by Bertlaolme. The ball was scrimmaged on the line, Ardwick having to save by touching down. Unsworth returned the drop out into touch, and from the line out the came player r Passed to Barnes (who had taken Belshaw's place at centre, i the Utter player going to full back), who made a short run and passed to Boardman. the latter putting in a good kick. From a scrimmage in the 'visitors' 25 Whittle passed to Barnes, who took a drop at goal. the ball going dead. From the drop out Barnes again got the ball and made a beauti- ful run, finishing up by a short kick, and Morris secured and sent the ball into touch. Cragan, Jone-, and Adamson were next to the front with a dribble, Pole havieg to kick dead. From the drop out Barnes secured the ball and ran through nearly the whole of his opponents, finishing by a good kick, Cragan following up had hard lines in not scor- ing. Some good passing between Whittle, Barnes, and Nevins was neutralized by the good tackling of Pole. Barnes again got hold from a pass by Whittle, and made another of his famous runs, and passed to the home forwards, but Bertholme stopped the rush. Brennan intercepted a pass from Whittle and kicked to Belshaw, who made his mark. Barnes taking the place, play again raged near the visitors' line. Morris passed to Henderson, who was finely collared by Jones, and then Whittle gave the hall to Barnes. who made a good attempt at goal, only missing by a few inches, Barnes again got hold from the drop out and ran the ball near the Ardwick line, Brennan relieving by a short punt, but Boardman returned, and, following up his kick, charged Bertholme off the ball, Molyneaux succeeding in grounding the leather over the line near the touch, Barnes failing at goal. Brennan re-started, and Barnes secured the ball and nut in a brilliant dodgy run, and the home forwards, led by Molyneaux, Cragan and Adamson, came through the scrimmage, the latter player taking the ball close to the line and could doubtless have scored but preferred to pass to Whittle, who had no difficulty in getting over, Barnes be- ing successful at the place. Shortly afterwards half time was called, the score standing Warrington two goals one try and three minor points, to Ardwick nothing. On resuming Whittle kicked off and Henderson punted to Barnes, who passed to Tones, this player paesi.ng forward. A scrimmage was formed, the ball being taken into touch. Adamson got possession from the line ?tat, and made a nice run and pass to Eyes, this player gaining, further ground before being collared by Bertholme. Whittle passed the ball to Barnes, who was collared by Pole, then Adamson and Hackett made a splendid dribble to the line, the latter player picking up passed behind him, thus enabling Hall to gain possession, who kicked to Ashurst, this player making a good return into touch. The visiting forwards now pulled themselves together a little, and made a grand dribble half the leegth of the fields the bell going into touch. The home front rank, however, worked-the ball back by .degrees, then Pole put in a strong run and kick, play resting in centre. Simp- son relieved to near centre, when the Warrington forwards, beaded by Eyes, Hackett, Craghan, and Jones dribbled close to the line, the last named player grounding the ball over the line, Barnes kicking a splendid goal. Henderson kicked off, and Barnes secured and put in is grand run and kick,

Hall returning into touch Drinkwater got hold from a pass by Morris, and sent the ball into touch. Whittle next gained possession and nassed nicely to Barns, who dropped a magnificient goal. Henderson kicked off and Barnes put in another dashing run, and the home forwards, by a com- bined dribble, sent the ball into touch near the line. After some give and take play Jones got the ball from a line out, and almost scored. Bertholme intercepted a pass and took play to centre, but the home forwards, headed by Moly- neaux, Thornley, and Adamson, worked the ball back again. Hall gained a free kick, but nothing became of it, then Barnes took another drop at goal, a minor resulting. Time being called leaving Warrington winners by 4 goals 1 try and 5 minor points, to Ardwick nil. Teams :—Warrington —Full back, Barnes; threquarter backs, Nevins, Belsbaw, and Boardman; half backs, Whittle (captain) and Bate ; forwards, Molyneaux, Adamson, Cragan, Ashurst, Jones, Eyes, Hackett, Unsworth, Tbornley„ Ardwicic—Full back. Hall ; tbreeqoarter backs, Pole, Drinkwater, and Bertholme; half backs, Brennan and Morris; forwards, Henderson, Morris, Webster, Simpson, Crawford, Morris, Buxton, Wood, Barber. WARRINGTON F.C.—PROPOSED JUNIOR COMPETITION.

With a view to making the Rugby game more popular in this district, and for the encouragement of junior clubs, the Warrington club propose to inaugarate a junior compe- tition, rules regarding which were on Tuesday evening drawn up by the Sub-committee, to be submitted to the General Committee at a meeting to be held next Monday. As at present proposed the whole of the games are to be played in the evenings, and a portion of the gates will be divided between competing clubs, and, after paying all ex- penses, the balance will be given to such charities, or other ieserviog objects, as the Committee of the Warrington F.C. may deem advisable. A gold centre medal will be given to each player of the winning team, and a silver medal to each player of the running up team. The coin- petition will be open to teams from bona fide clubs playing in Warrinpton, Sankey, Latchford, Orford, Winwick, Pad- gate, Stockton Heath, Grappenhall. and Walton. Each club desirous of competing must, according to present arrangements, give notice to the Secretary of the Warring- ton club, on or before the 13th of April. The draw for the first round will probably take place on the 15th, one representative of each competing club being allowed to be present. The entrance feels Sc each, and the matches will commence on the 18th of April. No player will be allowed to assist two clubs in the contest, and the games will be de- cided by points, in accordance with the rules laid down for the West Lancashire competition. All particulars may be had of the Secretary of the Warrington club.

div.head: SHIP CANAL AND THE JUBILEE.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL AND THE JUBILEE.

Sir,—We hear a lot of talk about what shall we do to celebrate the Queen's Jubilee. One town is going to do one thing, another town something else. If I arm not too late I should like to say, as a workingman, that I think that the beat way to celebrate the Jubilee would be not to spend so much money on one day's pleasure, as is the case in a large number of towns, but that the money be put to what will hod work for the hundreds of men that are walking about, and which wonld do a great deal to revive the trade of Warrington and all Lancashire, I mean the Ship Canal. Let those who have charge of the ways and means for the celebration look to this, and I think they will have the thanks and blessings of hundreds of men and women who are able and willing to work but cannot get it. Ido not mean that the women would make the canal, but they would be thankful that the husband was getting that which would enable them to find food for their children.
Hoping that you will be able to put this in your paper, and some friend will take the matter up for us poor work- log-men,-1 remain, dear sir, yours Stn. SPATE.
MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

Sir,—Numerous inquiries having been made as to the liability of shareholders in this company, I am instructed, with your permission, to state that the liability of a share- holder is absolutely limited to the amount remaining un- paid upon the shares he holds. The company cannot, as has been suggested, be styled "Limited." as it is not formed under what are known as the Limited Companies Acts. It is incorporated under its own stottcial Act of Par- liament by the name of "The Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany." A simple explanation of the matter is that the company is in this respect in exactly the same position as a railway company. It has also been frequently suggested by correspondents and others that the cipital of the company should be divided into £l, instead of £lO shares. This is. however, impracticable, as the Act of Parliament provides that the capital of the company shall consist of £lO shares, and Parliataent declined to sanction shares of smaller amount.—l am, &C.. A. H. WHITWORTH, Secretary. Manchester. March 23.

THE LIBRARY QUESTION AT WARRINGTON. Sir,— Would you allow me space in the next issue to say a few words in reference to the various schemes that baye been brought prominently before the public of Warrington to commemmorate her Majesty's Jubilee Year. The efforts of Mr. Morris and those who are working with him to make our library a free lending one, are deserving of all praise; and it is the wisit of hundreds of workingmen in this town, that he will not relax his efforts to obtain what we so much desire, namely, to be able to borrow books from the Library and take them home to read. It would confer one of the greatest blessings on us and our children that could be con- ferred. I can assure you, sir, there is no lack of interest shown by the working class in this subject, but on the contrary. every effort that is made is watched with keen in- terest, and careful note made of any frivolous objections that are made. This scheme has now been before the public of Warrington upwards of eight months. A Town's Meet- ing was called by the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Harrison), I over which he presided, when several schemes were brought forward and discussed, the Library scheme along with the rest. Afterwards they were put to the meeting, when the Free Lending Library scheme was carried unanimously. I cannot understand why these objections are constantly raised against the expressed wish of the ratepayers. We are told by Mr. Morris and others interested in this matter that the money derived from the penny in the pound is sufficient to meet the expenses of management. The Pres- ton ratepayers find a penny rate quite sufficient to pay for managing the Library, Museum, and Art Gallery. Icm assure you, sir, it is the earnest wish of hundreds of fami- lies in this town that the objections to the Free Lending Library scheme will soon be removed. We are desirous of enjoying the comfort of reading at home the books which are beat calculated to instruct our minds and raise us from the Slough of Despond.—Yours drc., JOHN SAXON. Bewaey-road, Warrington, March 24th, 1887.

div.head: SANITARY MATTERS IN WABRINGTON.
div.p: SANITARY MATTERS IN WABRINGTON.

Sir,—We have heard a good deal lately about the pre- eminent positien Warrington holds in the sanitary world, and I dare say many people who do not live here will think its sanitary arrangements quite a model. The sanitary policy of thote in authority has been very heroic, as we know, but like most heroic policies it has its drawbacks. It has given an egotistical alderman an opportunity of glorify- ing himself, and, as was generally anticipated by those who knew, he has not let the opportunity pass unimproved. The drawback has been that while attention has been so much fixed on great undertakings the ordinary sanitary concerns seem to have been very much neglected. The result is that I should think the inhabitants of Warrington, taking them all round, are better acquainted with the qualitiee—l mean the odoriferous, and utterly sickening qualities—of sewer gas than the inhabitants of most other towns. There are grids in the street that at certain hours let out such disgusting emanations that when one gets into their neighbourhood one instinctively takes in a long breath, as if for a dive, and then gets past them as quickly as possible. The grids might be excused if we could keep the baleful vapours out of our houses, but in very many instances this cannot be done, the gases in some cases seeming to have impregnated the very ground on which the houses are built. But what suggested this epistle was the record in your last week's paper of a death which is suspected to have been in some way due to unlit water from a well. One can hardly credit that in a town of the sanitary pretensions of Warrington any of Its inhabitants still draw their water supply from wells. Now that the " big thing" is out of the way, it is to be hoped that these smaller matters will engage the at- tention of the sanitarians, or our bo.sted death-rate—which after all is not so very small—will again be nothing to boast of.

div.head: SUFFERER.
div.p: A SUFFERER.
THE JUBILEE CELEBRATION.

Sir,—Being a Warringtonian, I naturally read with in- terest anything appertaining to my native town. lam glad to see that there is an evident desire to celebrate this year In as suitable a manner as possible, but yet it is with a pang of regret that I find it has been decided to leave the ques- tion of enlarging the Baths to the "remote future." It has everheen thus with the Baths, and I can remember distinct- ly that it has been the intention for the last six years at least, of the Baths Conamittee, to have the Baths enlarged, but the scheme seems as far off as ever. To celebrate the Jubilee by proc-ssions is all very well, but I cannot say that the money they will cost, will be the hest way of spending it, as they will simply give a plea- sure for a day. As regards the Park scheme I think the idea a good one, and one which ought to have been carried out years ago, but yet I must say that I entertain the no- tion, (which I observe the minority of the Jubilee General Committee did also) that the Baths question is a far more urgent one. It would have been a more " usefnl scheme," and therefore calculated to be of more benefit to the town. The meat that can be said of the Park scheme is that when carried out, it will be "pleasing to the eye." Warrington is sadly in need of good baths. The present ones are greatly inadequate to the wants of the town, and do not anything like meet the demand made upon them. I have often seen as many as 50 persons endeavouring to have a clean bath, and I have been given to understand that as many as 200 (if not more) have visited the Baths on a Sunday morning, so anyone can imagine the state and colour the water gets, and I know I have gazed upon it several times, and as it was not of its original colour have come away, and have noticed others do likewise. However, as public attention on the question seems to have been aroused lam yet in hopes that the Baths Committee will in the course of the next few months persuade the Council to adopt the " plan " soma years ago designed, and that there- fore Warrington will have baths worthy of the town, so that both sexes may indulge in a " water refresher "to their "bodies content."—Yours truly*, Seacombe, 24th March, 1887.
E. ENGLAND.

THE IRISH PRIESTS. I accept them on the faith engendered within Warrington, March 31st, 1887. S. DAVIES. Ime by finding such as! have verified to be as they stated. , The difference between tbe facts of geology and the state- ment of Moses, is that the former are even now accessable and capable of demonstration, whilst the statements are— well, merely statements—belied by the facts. . Again, I am asked if I can "sanely contend that one mind in a hundred, or one in a bundred thousand, can as- certain these facts for himself ?" No, probably net ; but may not exactly the same be said as to the interpretation of the Bible and its revision. I presume that even Mr. Gandy , has to rely upon mem more learned than himself for what' he knows of Scripture. So in both cases ignorant folk must rely upon their more learned fellows for their know- ledge of Scripture and science and the relation ot the one to the other. Then again, he disclaims 'my imputation that he, and such as he, try and " tinker " the word of God so as to make it square with the revelations of scienee. Now Daw- son, his great authority, but not the president of the Royal Society—does this. He and all other Reconcilers of Scrip- ture with geology, know there is not the remotest chance of even the semblance of an agreement between the facts of geology and the Six day statement—of Moses. So they "tinker" the six days into six—periods! Just fancy an eveaing and a.morning to a' period! "Whom the gods would destrofthey first make mad." Surely there must be an unseating of the reasonine faculties ere such an Impious and irrational idea would be entertained. For what does it mean? This :—We believe this to be the Word of God. In it He says that He created the world in six days. But this cannot be so. Ile must either have said what He did not mean or mean 'what he did not say, i.e., in effect, these blind expounders accuse the All Wise of (1) ignorance in the use of language, or(2) a desire to deceive. Now this is a very pretty dilemma; if the words of the Bible are right geology proves it to be wrong—where as if the words of Genesis I i 19 are wrong—as the pious Reconciler says —the authority of the whole book is impaired. In fact this blundering "tinkering " of what ought (to them) be the sacred writing, and above mutilation or correction by mortal hands, is only a means of getting these impious and illogical meddlers out of the frying pan of Scriptural error into the fire of Biblical destruction. But Mr. Gandy still maintains " that Moses has not been disproved." You may take a horse to the pond but you can- not make him drink—so a person devoid of the logical faculty may not be able to sea how undoubted facts dis- prove unfounded statements, In conclusion I will offer Mr. Gaedy one more disagree- ment between Moses and modern science. j may say that the facts mentioned belong to the sciences of geology and archreelogy, while the application of them as a test of the accuracy of Moses' etitetnent I am alone responsible for. It has never before, to my knowledge, appeared in print. All modern writers on prehistoric man agree that locg ere the use of metals was known, or the art of working them discovered, there were two stone-using ages. The old stone age of rough chipped flints, and a succeeding one—the new stone—of polished stone axes, hammers, drc. A glance through such works as Lubbock's "Aptiquity of Man," orJoly's " Man before metals" will show that man for long ages must have been exclusively a flint or stone implement- using being, a hunter with only these primitive weapons for offence and defence. This in, or near, historic times was succeeded by an age of bronze implements, and lastly, that again by ours of iron. Now if Mr. Gandy will refer to Gera. iv., 22, he will find Moses stating that brass and iron were forged or wrought and that during the early part of the life of Adam, the first created man—circa A.M. 160. Now, to say nothing about the suspiciously early appearance of braes upon the scene, iron is a very difficult metal to smelt, and required the accumulated experience of centuries to subdue its stubborn nature and make it the obedient servant of man, which it has now become. Now here is a collision between the facts and the statement. Which must give way? Let every man answer for himself. The highly paid officials of our "National Church" are silent on this matter. Does silence give consent ? Are they too wise, or too indifferent to give us an authoritative opinion on this grave question? If their thousands per annum depended upon it we should hear noise enough. If the views I take of these matters be erroneous let the error be made manifest —otherwise let them be accepted. Let the truth prevail I am, sir, your obedient servant,
JOHN PEERS.
Penketb, 28th March, 1887.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse,Whiston, on Thurs- day forenoon, when there were present Mr. John Lowe (chairman), Rey. Thomas Chambers, Rev, C. W. Wooll, Rev. Dean Finegan; Messrs. Joseph Jackson, James Buck- ley, Joseph Ellison, William Middlehurat, Peter Middlesex, Charles B. Johnson, J. Fisher, J. Matthews, J. Burchall, E. Syder, W. ryrer, J. Ranson, R. A. Graves, T. Eatock, J. Leatherbarrow, J. W. Wareing, S. H. Hartley (clerk) STATISTICS.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 492 inmates, against 496 last week, and 512 in the corresponding period of last year. THE MEASLES AND VAOCINATION.—The Local Govern. ment Board have assented to the postponement of the April vaccinations in the Woolton district in consequence of a serious outbreak of mnasles.—The Clerk stated that he had issued notices in Woolton to this effect. THE EMIGRATION OF CHILDREN TO CANADA.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that consequent on the non-receipt of information as to the ad- dresses of children sent out to Canada under the Board's order of the 16th June, 1884, they requested the Guardians to take such farther steps as might be necessary to enable them to furnish the Board with the names of the persons with whom were placed the children who were sent out under the care of the Rev. Mr. Whelan, and others under the care of the Rev. T. H. Fildes.—The Clerk said the Rev. Dean Finegan had kindly promised to assist him in his in- quiries.—On the motion of Mr. James Fisher, seconded by Mr. Leatherbarrow„ a resolution was unanimously carried authorising Dean Finegan to assist the Clerk in making such inquiries.—Mr. Leatherbarrow said he supposed it was understood that the Board would not send any more chil- dren to Canada until the information was obtained.—The Chairman and Clerk both replied that they should think not.

THE MILE QUESTION.—The Clerk stated that with regard to the resolutions passed at the last meeting remitting the tines of the milk contractors, Mr. Philip Lowcock and Mr. 0. Ward, he had prepared a letter to be sent to the Local Guvernment Board. It was stated in it that the effect of the resolutions would be to pay the sum of £39 145 to Mr. Lowcock, the present contractor, and £4B us 9d to Mr. Ward, the late contractor. £2O 16s 6d of the £39 14s, and the whole of the £4B lie 91 were beyond the time of pay- ment as prescribed by the 22nd and 23rd Vic., cap. 49, section 1. He (the clerk) was not aware that the Guardians had power to modify any conditions of a contract they might have entered into without the consent of the Local Government Board—lt was resolved that the letter be sent to the Local Government Board.—A long letter on the sub- ject was read from Mr. W. Middlehurst, of St. Ann's, St. Helens, who said he thought the breakina of the contract without reasonable grounds would form a precedent which would give much trouble in the future.

div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

On Saturday the semi-finals for the Yorkshire cup were played. Leeds St. John and Liyersedge met on the ground of the Leeds Parish Chureh club, and t he game was wit- nessed by about 8,000 spectators. A. hot contest took place with the result that St. John won by seven minors to three miners. Wakefield Trinity and Ossett were the ether corn- peting teams their encounter taking place at Dews- bury, in the presence of about 6,000 spectators. The Mini- tarians managed to come out victorious by one goal, one try, and four minors to Oasett three minors. Wakefield Trinity and Leeds St. John will, therefore, meet in the •final. . _ _

The great event amongst the Associationists on Saturday was the final tie in the Lancashire cup competition between the Bolton Wanderers (holders) and Preston North End. Owing to the varied fortune which has attended the several meetinzs of the two clubs in ordinary fixtures, only so late as the previous Saturday the Wanderers registering a clever victory over the North 'Enders. additional interest was given to the event. after a start was made the game progressed some little time without either getting the upper hand, until Drummond and J. Roes attacked the Wanderers' goal. Relief came from " hands " by Drummond, and give-and- take play followed. Then Ross and Thomson raced down into the Bolton quarters, and Dewhurst put in a shot that Trainer failed to atop. Three times almost in a minute the Wanderers' goal-keeper was tested, and with the fourth shot Dewburst beat him. The home players had now a spell of advantage, and attacked fiercely, but the defence was up to Ithe occasion, and just on the cell of half-time a coiner fell to North End, and Drummocd placing well to J. Ross, the latter placed a third goal to the credit of North End. The second portion of the game was fiaelV contested, though the greater part of the preesure was done by the Prestohians. Trainer defended in a marvellous manner, and prevented any 'further score, the cup goinz to Preston by three goals to nothing. There were about 14,000 parsons present to wit- ness the game, and the receipts were £335. Aspull, the runners-up of last year, are now the posses- sors of the West Lancashire Cup, having beaten Wigan, the runners-up of this year, by twenty points to one. The final contest between these clubs was brought off on Satur- day on the Fairfield Athletic Ground, there being about 6,000 spectators present. From the beginning to the end, but more particularly in the latter half, the Wigan team were oyerweighted bY their opponents. After the game the cup was presented to the victors by the Mayor of Liver= pool.

div.head: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.
div.p: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.

TIF OWD QUACK. If yo've ever gone ramblin rea.wnd the Merkut, Yo'll ha' clapped yor een oft tort th' owd Quack. He stood mony a day wi' his nostrums, Drest in an owd suit o' grey black. He'd o sorts o' roots, herbs an' mixtur's ; An'd coff -drops he oft livered reawnd To th' creawd as gaped on him i' wonder As he speawted wi' thunner-like seawnd. - On his stall he'd booath smo an' big bottles 0' fizzic for cowds, corns an' worms! Wi' pill boxes heeaped i' one corner— His pills kilt disease an' id germs! He co'd 'em his own manufacture; Aw'd ne'er back his statement wi' brass; For, when aw kept rapputs wi' th' shuffle, Aw've pitched sitch like pills among th' 'ass! If yo've heeard him aw'll bet as yo shivered, As diseases he wandered among; For he'd din 'em o eawt rotashun 'Till slaver fair dript fro' his tongue! An' he'd rattle off gradely jaw-squelchers, Clitter chatter. But nob'ry cud tell Wod he'd bin tawkin' o'er when he'd finished— An' he wornd a bit wiser hissel I I' phrenology sometimes he dabbled; One merkut-day he wur agate Wi' a youngster o' owd Skennin' Allse's, An' fingered his bump-lumps fost rate. "There's something to puzzle the sages I' this urchin's head!" th' owd Quack sed. An', hi th' way, as awed sin thad lad scrattin', Aw raylee believe as he lied! He wur ravin' eawt once abeawt th' toothache, When a cute Cheshire cbap, co'd "Dry Dick," Clapt his hand to his jaw o o'th' sudden. Th' Quick sheawted, "You've nothin' but tic!— Take this mixture!" Dick looked at him simple, An' pocketed th' stuff reight away, Then sed, “'Twur a fleck as wur bitin' But tick's chep,—aw' thank tha. Goody!" Th' owd quack wur as mad as a hornet At bein' so nicely taen In; But seem' o th' folk re,awnd him laffin, He joined wi a good hearty grin. When a strappin' lad sed he'r consumptive, ('Twur a gradely wed relished skit;) His mam sed if his teeth kept consumin' So mitch, he'd to find th' grub—or flit Aw never wur sucked with his-"humbugs," Tho' often he tried th' best he cud. Aw ne'er heeard he'd kilt fooak vii fizzle Aw kornd say he ever dud good ' But this aw con say—streyt and truthful— Aw've heeard mony a gassin' chep jack Tell " buzzes ;" but th' champion truth-ratcher As licked o beside wur th' owd Quack! JACK 0' ANN'S.
ATTACK ON A 111AIL`DRIVEIL-SUICIDE OF THE ASSAILANT.

A shocking affair took place on Saturday m°l between Boxmoor Station and Hemel Hempstead. 7.g Bailey, mail carrier, had conveyed the night. mails to Bozmoor Station, and was returning with the morning mails to Hemel Hempstead about four a.m., when, in passing over a bridge, he was struck by a man on the head and partially stunned. Several shots were then fired, but fortunately these lodged in the mail bags. Bailey shouted for assistance, and his assailant ran away. On arriving at Hemel Hampstead about five o'clock, Bailey informed the police of the occur- rence, and Police-sergeant Moyley and Constable Pear. man proceeded to the residence of a young man named George Norris, living in Chapel-street The man opened the upstairs window, apparently with a revolver in his hand, but did not fire. He closed the window, and screams and two reports of a pistol were immediately heard. The door was burst open, and on the police going upstairs they saw Norris getting out of the back window on to the roof of an outhouse. They gave chase, but failed to overtake him. His dead body was afterwards discovered in the river Gade. Norris's wile, who was found to have received two bullet wounds, woe con- veyed to West Herts. Infirmary. An inquest was held on Monday on the body of Norris. The mail carrier, Bailey, in examination' said that on Friday evening Norris accompanied him to the mail' apparatus on the railway, and asked questions about the mails. Norris about two years ago acted as mail carrier. Witness described Norris's attack upon him as he was retunain., next morning with the mails. James Townsend, blacksmith, said he saw the deceased running across the field in his shirt to Gradebridge Park, and jump into the water. Witness followed on horse- back, but did not attempt to get the deceased out of the water. The body was allowed to remain in the water until the police arrived. A revolver was found at the spot. Mr. Russell Steel, surgeon, said he attended Mrs. Norris, and found a wound near the right ear, and another on the right arm, and extracted a bullet from the latter. The unfortunate woman had since been de- livered of twin children, both dead. She was now pro- gressing favourably. The jury returned a verdict of fele de se, and censured the witness Townsend for not attempting to remove Norris's body from the water.

div.head: MARKET QUESTION.
div.p: THE MARKET QUESTION.

Sir,—lt is understood that at the next meeting of our Town Council this qaestion will again come up for con- sideration, and I have learned with the deepest regret that 1 the Markets Committee have, by the casting vote of its chairman, decided to allow the present arrangement to con- tinue. It will be remembered that at the last Councill meeting a recommendation was upon the minutes of the Market Committee that the farmers' wives and daughters I (the egg and butter people) were to he removed back again I to the Market Hall, their old position, from whicli tkey were removed against their will. At the last moment this was withdrawn for re-consideration. Since this meeting memo- rials have been presented to the committee of an excep- tionally numerous and influential character. All the trades- men in the four principal streets around Market-gate have, with one solitary exception, appended their names. The farmers and their wives, to the number of one hundred and, thirty genuine tenants of the Market, have petitioned ask- I ing for their removal to the Market Hall. The butchers,, who at present are the only tenants of the hall, have also unanimously asked that this arrangement be carried out. Now,! would ask, in fairness to the petitioners, what diffi- culty can there possibly be in complying with so reasonable a request; and if the Market Committee could:see their way a month ago to recommend what they are now asked to carry out, has anything occurred since to justify this change of policy? The Market Hall, which was erected at an enormous cost to the ratepayers, is at present almost tenantless, and the few remaining tenants will, I predict, leave within the next three months if this alteration is not made. I tail to see that it will make any material differ- ence in the new Market, because it is extremcly difficult at the present time for a local tradesman to obtain a stall if he desires one, and the removal, by their own consent, of the country people would provide greater accommodation for the dealers in dry goods, a class often- ante which the Market Committee seem desirous of afford- ing every facility to. I trust that the members of our Town Council will give this matter their most earnest con- sideration. The tradesmen of Warrington have ever been loyal and constant in their support of every movement in. aogarated for the public good by our corporation. During these recent years of commercial depression no class of the community has suffered more than the shop- keepers, many of whom have had to toil early and late for the purpose of reducing expenses and paying their way. I can assure the Town Council that the keenest interest is being taken in this question, and their decision on Tues- day next is awaited most anxiously, and with deep con- cern by a large and important body of ratepayers, who have confidence in their representatives, knowing they will re- spect their opinions and honestly endeavour to discharge their responsible duties for the public good—Yours, ' A TRADESMAN, March 31, 1857.

div.head: PLEA FOR IRELAND.
div.p: A PLEA FOR IRELAND.

_ Sir,—Wlll you kindly allow me to say a word for Ire- land ? I would also say something more than a word to our Dissentient Liberal friends. Were I capable, I would pray them in the strongest language ever used, to consider before it is too late, whither they are being hurried. Does past experience go for nothing? Is it not true that since 1832, when the back of Whigism was broken, that the stream of Lib-ralism has flowed surely on, carrying with it amelioration of the masses? Can our Dissentient friends, that is the Radical portion, remember a time when they were in sympathy with Conservatism? Or is it that they are now willicg to close their eyes to tke teachings of the past? Surely net; they know—Teries are never expected to know—that the environments and circumstances of life chaege with each succeeding day's work. . . _ . _ .

WFiat has the Toryism of—Warrington to commend it for acceptanCe to our local Dissentients? In what does it differ from tho Toryism found ina other towns? In nothing; it is now as it has always been, a slavish subservience to the fascinations of power, and where power is unattainable, to place. Mr. Balfour has proved in his speech, introduc- ing the new Coercion Bill, that Toryism can be original only when showing its fangs. Let those who seem to prefer the lead of Mr. Cham- berlain ask themselves what it is they are following? Is there anything definite, anything practical? I, for one, say if there is anything definite, let us have it tabled so that we may compare it with the definite and practical measures placed before the country by Mr. Gladstone. Lord Salis- bury betrayed in his Newport speech a doubt as to the effi- cacy of coercion. Did he not ask his audience—" Are von quite certain, in the first place, that the Crimes Act would have prevented what is taking place flow?" Further on, in the same speech, he said—" The Crimes Act did not diminish outrages ;" and he further declared that the Crimes Act " was no restraint on boycotting." More than this, he urged as an excuse for not renewing the Crimes Act that it "would have produced so intense an exaspera- tion amongst the Irish people that you would have pro- duced ten times more evil, ten times more resist- ance to law than your Crimes Act, even if it had been renewed, would possibly have been able to check." Still, with all this knowledge of Ireland's justly rooted aversion to sit any longer under English law, we have the initiatory step taken for—not Lord Salisbuy's twenty years—but to use Mr. Balfour's words, "We do not propose it should be limited in point of time." Can the headstrong folly of a party go any further? Is it this that has caused Liberals to respond to the feeble cry—" Come over and help us." In what does Mr. Gladetone's proposition differ from the sentiment now running in men's minds? He proposes to give a Parliament on well defined lines to Ireland. What is thought desirable is "a large council chamber, with the power given to members to work out such a policy as would result in Ireland's happiness." So we see practical Radi- cals running after the Tories bolstering up a false sentiment, grasping at the shadow, and losing the substance. The main question is this—ts Ireland likely to rest content with an indefinite term of coercion, and is such an abominable and outrageous system of ruling a portion „if the United Kingdom Hirai,- to make any remedial measures accept- abl& to the Irish? I say no, and I ask Dissentient Liberals for their answer. •

Nobody pretends that the millennial has come, or that the condition of the people is by any means all that could be desired. [ . .... A peasant in County Meath, going by train to some races, was accosted by his priest, who asked him his destination. On being told it, he said, "You are going to destruction." " Well, if I am, your reverence,' said Tim, suiting the action to the word, "I have got a return- ticket, and here it is." HE wes THE MAN.—A stranger in Maine desired to enter into negotiations with a farmer' in a town in that State for the nuiChase of some live-stock. Meeting a man driving an ox-waggon, the stranger inquired, "Can you inform me where Mr. West thres?" "There are a number of West,s living about here. Which one do you mean ?" "This one owns some fine oxen," "They all own pretty line oxen." "I don't know this man's Christian name; but he has oxen for sale." "I guess any on *era would sell if they could get their price." "Yes; but this Mr. Wear Is wealthy." "They're all forehanded." "But this' West is said to be a dose-fisted man and hard at a bargain." "They air all of them kind of close-fisted." "Well, ; don't know that I can give any other quality by which you will know 'which West lam after. Oh, yes! I did hear that there was a story afloat that this West once robbed his own brother's hen-roost !" said the traveller, laughing, "Of course it was only a story." The ox-driver smiled grimly. "Wall, stranger, he said slowly, "I reckon I'M the man !" A certain noble Scottish lord used to go about Naples attended by a large ferocious bull-dog. Having decided upon going to Rome, he proceeded to the station and took his place in a first-class carriage, the " dawg " taking up a position on a seat opposite its master. The platform-inspector, with many gesticulations, declared that the bull-dog should not travel in a passenger car- riage. "Very well, then, take him out!" was Lord X.'s quiet rejoinder. In vain the official expostulated; Lord X. merely reiterated his former reply—a piece of advice which was not followed,; and, apparently master of the situation, he threw himself back in his seat and calmly lighted a cigar. But the Italians were not to be outdone, and, quietly detaching the carriage in which the "Eng- lish milor " was seated,, they made up the train with another baggage car andstarted it off. Lord X. sat quietly smoking for a quarter of an hour, and then, sun. prised at the delay-, thrust his head out of the window and demanded when the train was going to start. His feelings, when the situation was described to him, may be imagined.

div.head: WHY, WOMEN 111AIIRY.
div.p: WHY, WOMEN 111AIIRY.

An article has been going the rounds of the press entitled, "Reason Why Men Marry." So I have begun to make inquiries why women marry. I began first on my landlady at dinner time, but she answered me so sourly, "Because I didn't stay single!" with a look that added "you idiot" plainly as words could have done, that I tremblingly made up my mind to pay up my last month's board-bill, and pursue further inquiries by post. So, to the question, "Why did you marry ?" the following answers wena received : " Because all fools weren't dead yet." •

"Because had the chance." "Because 1 didn't want to be a hired girl. I soon found out, though, that I was working for my board and clothes." "I threatened him with a breach of promise suit if he wouldn't. "Because I wore so much store hair and bought my complexion he thought I was 24 instead of 42." "Because I never wanted to go into any business where I couldn't be boss." "Because I was as big a fool as most other girls are." "Because he always said I was an angel. Now he always says he wishes I was one." "To see who was the best man. I've found out / am." "Out of pride fo4. my sex. He had already outlived three women. I have brought back the palm to my sex. He was my first husband, and I am looking for my sixth." If there is any woman who reads this paper who married for love, money or spite, write quickly and let me know; or if any such case has come under your notice, please inform me and 'you will be suitably rewarded.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Gibson, Blackhurst, Jolley, Voisey. Bonnell, Ratcliffe, Brown, Isherwood, Derbyshire, Wright, W. Hough- ton, Clarke, Eckersley, Kilshall, J. Houghton, .1-0. Sutton (clerk) and S. Sutton, (assistant clerk) .

div.head: WORKHOUSE MASTER.
div.p: THE WORKHOUSE MASTER.

--„ Mr. GIBSON asked if the workhouse master had complied with the order of the Board by giving up his books, Etc.— The CLERK said the books were not yet,quite finished ; the books had to be prepared for the audit. Mr. Batowx said they were perfectly satisfied with the matter up to that moment.—The subiec., then dropped.

div.head: -SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.
div.p: -SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.

This Committee recommenaled that the tender for leather of Messr.3. Abel and Pickavance, be accepted, it being the lowest local tender.—On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, se- conded by Mr. ISHERWOOD, the minutes were passed.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES.

The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 99 cases, 85 of which were old and 14 new cases.—Mu. BL&CHEURST moved the adoption of the min- utes—Mr. Istakitwoon, in seconding, asked if in any of the 14 cases recently brought before the magistrates fees had been allowed by the Cemmittee.—Mr. BLACKHURST said the Committee had had no information to that effect.—Mr. Jot.. LEY said that iii regard to some of these cases that came be- fore the Committee it would be impossible to answer such a question as that of Mr. Isherwood. The CLERK sugges- ted that as they would soon be re-appointing their Commit- tees Mr. Isherwood might be put on the School Fees Committee. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The subject then dropped. HOUSE andmirrimE.
This committee recommended the adoption of the tender for groceries of Messrs. W. Owen and Sons, and on the motion of Mr. &rows, seconded by Mr. JoLLEY,the minutes were adopted.

div.head: LETTER FROM DR. JACK.
div.p: LETTER FROM DR. JACK.

The CLERK read the following letter from Dr. Jack "42, Church-treet, Warrington, 29th March, 1887. Dear sir, I enclose you a cutting from the Warrington "Examiner " wn:.ch possibly refers to myself, and which may have been read by some of the Guardians. I have placed the matter in the hands of a solicitor who has elicited that the writer of it is a clerk of the name of Davies in the em- ploy of Thewlis and Griffiths, of Mersey-street, and whose residence is in Knutsford-road, Latchford. It would give me great pleasure if any of the Guardians would honour me with a visit when I would be glad to demonstrate to them the arrangements I have madetor the comfort of the poor. —Yours faithfully, R. M. JACK. J. C. Button, Esq.”—Mr. JOLLBY said he was very glad to hear Dr. Jack's letter read. He thought it was a sufficient reply to the letter it referred to. which was in very 'lowery language.—Mr. ISHERWOOD said he had passed down Church-street as much as anybody, but he had never seen anything of the kind referred to. He had never seen the people outside.—Mr. DARBYSHIRB thought the letter cast a reflection on the doctor which was unnecessary, and he thought the manner and pint of it was wrong.—The CHAIRMAN said that any of the Guardians who chose might accept Dr. Jack's invitation to see the ,place.—The subject then dropped.—The relief cases were then taken.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON'. THURSDAY._

It would be a mistake to suppose from the hysterical leaders in the "Times" that polities at Westminster are in a seething state, and that it is only by the sharp exercise of authority that men are prevented from seizing each other by the throat. The " Times " is, appropriately for the season, as mad as a March hare. Englishmen who live at home at ease, and kncw nothing of the ferocity of sectarian temper in Belfast or Derry, will gather from the leading articles in the "Times" a very fair notion of how Orangeism raves in sight of its tra- ditional enemy. By the recently introduced prac- tice of uplifting the veil of anonymity that used to pertain to the press, it is well-known that the gentleman who writes these ferocious rhapsodies is an Irish Orangeman; and truly he behaves as such. We must go back to the time when the late Lord Beaconsfield was a casual contributor to the press, to find anything like the tone now adopted by what is humorously called "the leading journal" in reference to Mr. Gladstone and the great party which is pledged to give home Rule to Ireland. But this is all their fun or their fury. There is no trace of this cut-throat ferocity in the House of Commons itself. The Parnellites, are, after their kind, pretty lively, and followed Mr. Balfour's speech with sarcastic and too audible commentary. But there is nothing like the personal ferocity' that was displayed towards Mr. Forster when, in quite other circumstances, he was charged with the duty of bringing in a Coercion Bill. One reason for this is that in 1881 the Parnellites were desperate, whilst to-day they are hopeful. Then, with mur- der and outrage prevalent in Ireland, they were discredited, and having no argument to offer in re- sistance to the proposal of the Government, were compelled to have recourse to noisy obstruction. Now it is the Government that is hopelessly in the wrong; yielding to evil partisan influence, they have brought in the most drastic Coercion Bill of the eighty-seven, at a time when, according to their own statistics, crime is diminishing in Ireland, and has almost reached the vanishing point. The Home Rulers are sure to win and therefore can afford to be light-hearted, while the Conserva- tives are depressed with the equal certainty of de- feat and are not in the mood for cock-crowing. Thus proceedings from night to night in the House of Commons are exceedingly prosaic, and interest is principally centered in conjecture as to when the debate may end. This is the state , of things to-day; but it may, I think, be safely predicted that the situation is likely to grow in intensity. The Liberal Opposition, outnumbered in the House by defection of the followers of Lord Hartington and Mr. Cham- berlain, intend to appeal to the country. Meetings are to be held in various centres of population, and the British nation is to be asked whether Ireland is to be coerced or conciliated.

The Queen's departure for the Continent at this critical time in politics adds something to the grow- ing difficulties of Ministers. Her Majesty now, as in Lord Palmerston's time, is most exigent in keep- ing up the farce elaborately started every session in the Queen's speech, which represents the Sover- eign in the first person singular as originator, directoress, and arbiter of all affairs of State. Some people might imagine that if Her Majesty could be spared for holiday visits to the Continent at the busiest time of the year, Ministers responsible to Parliament for the conduct of affairs might be left to direct them ostensibly as they do actually. But the Queen does not take that view. She insists upon personally perusing all documents of import- ance. Accordingly, every morning a special mes- senger will be depatched to Cannes or Aix-les-Bains with a box of papers. Moreover, a Cabinet Minister will have to leave his business, wllich, if it ia any- thing. should he very important, to attend upon Her Majesty in her holiday retreat. This flight from London at the opening of the season is, by the way, only the beginning of a procedure which vexes the soul of the London tradesman, whose loyalty is broad-based upon a demand for his com- modities, which rises or falls with the movements of the Court. The Queen will return from the Con- tinent the last week in April, and after a brief stay at Windsor will proceed to Balmoral, return- • ing just in time for the Jubilee Celebration, which • concluded she proceeds straightway to Osborne. I Those who owe Alfred Tennyson many hours of intellectual delight—and the range of debtors is very wide—have from time to time during the past ten years tried to think that with the last produc- tion from the veteran Poet Laureate's. pen the lowest point of the ebbing tide of his power had been marked. It really seemed that Lord Tenny- son could not do anything worse than the hysterical scolding about the Fleet, or the more elaborate wordiness of the continuation of Locksley Hall. But alas! the Jubilee has been his ruin, as it promises to be that of other personages. It is a long time since anything has been published so puerile as the prose fantastically printed in the current issue of "Macmillan," and called "A Jubilee Ode." It is original only in its sheer pitifulness. Where, in the last stanza, the lines run more smoothly, there is.a gross plagiarism which instantly strikes the recollection.

"Are there thunders moaninz in the diotasoe ? Are there spectres movin in the darkness ?" What is this but an echo of the well-known episode in the "Heathen Chißee ?" " Do I sleep, do I dream, do I wonder and doubt? Are things what they seen,, or are visions about?" It is a thousand pities that there is not someone strong enough and wielding sufficient authority to take care of the splendid reputation which Lord Tennyson has ot late been trifling with.

I It is reported that Macmillans gave the Poet Laureate one hundred guineas for the Ode, which, to take a liberal view of its intrinsic value, is at least two hundred and forty times in excess. But ma curious way the investment is turning out to be quite a Guinness or a Hotchkiss. It may have been observed that all the London morning papers save one contented themselves with giving extracts from the Ode. The "Daily News," probably enam- oured of the excellence of the literary Work, gave it in full. This was, however, an infringement of the copyright law, by which a publisher of a former casual contribution by the Poet Laureate had pro- fited. Of a poetical contribution, running to a hun- dred verses, newspaper editors may if their readers will stand it, quote ninety-nine with impunity. If they add the huneredth they come under the action of the law. The example of the "Daily News" was followed in the afternoon by the "St. James's Gazette" and the "Echo," the publication being promptly followed by the appearance of the solici- tor to Messrs. Macmillan, who demanded a cheque for £5O, upon pain of action for damages being forthwith raised. The money was, I believe, in each case forthcoming, there 'being no legal ex- cuse for an obvious breach of the law. Many of the country papers yesterday fell into the same trap, and whatever the public may think of the Poet Laureate's Ode, his publishers will have no reason to regret their connection with it as a commercial transaction. The infernal machine—a bottle an inch and a half long, and the circumference of a lead pencil— posted to Mr. Arthur Balfour, has not created in the House of Commons that shock of terror which might have been expected. It is, indeed, whispered that the whole business is an ebullition of humour from the Irish camp, where 'the boys" are accus- tomed to vary the gravity of imperial politics by pranks of various kinds. The great dramatic event of the week has been the production of "Man and Wife" on Tuesday night. I have not seen the theatre so full since the Langtry days. It was an audience of the most fashionable first-nighters. The Prince was there in great state, and everyone was excited to see what this new actress would be like. A timely issue of photographs flooded the shop windows Monday, Mrs, Brown Potter is distinctly a Pri on nce k
