div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 2, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 2, 1887.

of Wales beauty. H.R.H. is no bad judge. He certainly made a great hit with the Langtry. He likes an exuberant generous type, and is not sym- pathetic to. mstheticism. He admired Mrs. Price, and Mrs. Wheeler, and Mrs. Langtry, and Miss Chamberlain, and he admires Mrs. Brown Potter. But, a prince's admiration does not make a Bernhardt. Everyone was curious to see what sort of an actress this beautiful American would turn out. Everyone got a surprise. I think the Prince looked more surprised than anyone else. In the first three acts she was as stagey and demonstrative as if she were a New Adelphi heroine of the old type. Towards the end of the play she got more quiet, and when she ceased to be noisy she really showed a treat deal of power and emotion, and the stuff out of which a great actress might be made. If her friends expected immediate triumph they are disappointed. Tuesday's performance would be called a success—but a success partly of curiosity, and partly of hope. It was a bright scene in the Theatre, but there followed elsewhere one much gayer. Mr. George Lewis gave in honor of the occasion a supper at his house in Portland-place, and thither after the play went all the principal personages both from before and behind the curtain. Mrs. Brown Potter was there, of course, looking a little tired after the violent exertions of the evening. The Prince of Wales arrived shortly after midmght and remained till after three o'clock. He would probably not have gone then only for a little incident. It is one of the privileges attendant upon the presence of Royalty in the social circle that no one may leave before Royalty goes, except by gracious permission. Towards three o'clock Mrs. Potter, who was evi- dently dead beat, approached 11.R.H., and dropping a pretty curtsey asked if she might go home. The Prince said "Yes," and the principal attraction of the party having withdrawn he himself with his suit speedily followed. But this did not break up the party, which did not disperse till four o'clock had struck. There was some singing by Arthur Cecil and George Grossmith, and some recitation by another well-known actor; but Mrs. Brown Potter, who is invariably called upon for a recitation on occasions similar to this, was naturally enough excused. It was a very joyous party, none enjoy- ing it more than our coming King.
PUBLIC
FRODSHAM.

LECTURE —A lecture, entitled '"the Carpenter's Son," was given in the United Methodist Free Church, Frodsham, on Monday evening, by the Rev J Lewis, in which he care. fully reviewed the whole character and work of Christ. The chair was taken by Mr Thomas Hough.

WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS—The final meeting of this class was held in Trinity School-room, on Friday evening, when the Rev. E. Mosscrop presided. The evening was taken up by part-songs and choruses by the choir, and songs, pianoforte solos, and readings by friends. Refreshments had been provided. Hearty votes of thanks were given to the president and Mr Mosscrop for their very valuable services to the class during the present and pre- vious year. Votes of thanks were aleo passed to Mr J. Kent, secretary, and to Mr J. Nicholas. treasurer. KINGSLEY MEN'S MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY—On Monday eveninz, the members of this society were enter- tained by the Vicar (Rev A P Reynolds), with a tea in the girls' schoolroom, the occasion being the last meeting of the class for the present. Afterward, a public gathering was held in the larger -echool-hosse. where a highly-interesting lecture was delivered by the Vicar of Frodsham (Rev H B Blogg, M.A.), concerning his recent tour in Canada and the States. The different places of interest visited by the rev. gentlemen were illustrated by means of dissolving views. PRESENTATION.—In consequence of the removal et the Rev E Charley, M.A., senior curate of the parish of Frod- sham, the teachers in connection with the Frodsham Church-street Sunday school, desiring to express their re- gret at losing Mrs Charley,*.who bas for a number of years past been a most regular teacher, have presented her with a very handsome four-fold screen, the height of which is sft. 9in.. each panel being richly embroidered with gold on black satin. Mr and Mrs Charley leave Frodsham much to the regret of many parishioners, and with every sincere wish for their future happiness and prosperity. MUSICAL Bomar's CONCERT.— On Wednesday evening the closing concert of the present season of the Frodsham Musical Society was given in the Town Hall to an appre- ciative. though not a large audience. The first part of the programme was taken up by selections from Handel's ova- torin, Samson.' The members of the society contributed seven choruses, all€l solos were sung by Mrs. Mosscrop, Miss E. E. Riley, and Miss K. S. Rigby; and Messrs. Webster, Williams, and Curnow. In the second part of the pro- gramme the members gave the part-songs, "The celebration of springs" and "The nightingale." Mrs. Mosscrop con- tributed a song, "The children's home ; " and by desire Miss E. E. Riley, "The kingdom blest." Messrs. Millward, Williams, Knowles. and Curnow gave the quartettes, "Strike the lyre" and "By Celia's Arbor." Mr. Charles Hibbert gave a pianoforte solo. Mr. Curnow was the conductor.

. • THE DISASTER AT A BAZAAR.—At the Liverpool County Court, on Tuesday, before his Honour Judge Thompson, the case of Tyrer v. Linaker was heard.—ln this case Messrs. Tyrer and Co., of 223, Deansgate, Manchester, were the plaintiffs. and Mr_ H. Cl:Linaker, of Frodsham, was the defendant; and the action, which had been sent down from the High Court for trial, was for the recovery of £47 6s 2d, for the hire of three tents and certain amusements, includ- ing marionettes and Punch and Judy. It appeared that in the sumnier of 1886 a committee, of which the defendant was the representative, arranged to hold a schools bazaar at Frodeham. Tents were duly erected, and the principal one was stocked with goods, but on the morning of the 14th a storm arose, which blew down the principal tent, causing a considerable dat...age for which the defendants now made a counter-claim of £50.--after hearing a number of witnesses, and the arguments of counsel, his Honour found for the defendants, who abandoned the counter-claim.

_ POLICE NEWS.—At Eddisbury Petty Sessions on Monday, the following cases were heard :—Threatening Language : Louisa Stubbs, of Rock Savage, was charged with using threatening language towards Pl.cehe Worrall, of Overton, on the 10th March. Stubbs was bound over to keep the peace for six months, and to pay the costs Ss 6J.— Assault : Thomas Spruce was summoned for assault. Emma Blythe, of Alvanley, stated that on the 26th February she ant, her husband were in the Railway Inn, Helsby, when the defend- ant commenced quarrelling, and the landlord put him out. On their way home they met defendant, who renewed the disturbance. He pushed witness about the road, made faces at them, and tantAlized them. Defendant also kicked her. Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months, and pay Ss 6d costs.—Drunkenness: The following persons were fined for drunkenness: Thomas Guest, farm labourer, for being drunk at Alv,.nley on the 23rd February. 5s and costs; Ann Whitby, of Frodslaam, for an offence at that place on the 19th March, 7e 63 and costs.— Without Licenses : James Walker and Caleb Welke., of Norley, were summoned for keeping dogs without licenses. Sergeant Marshall proved the cases. Defendants were fined 5s each and costa.

div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.]
23, Old Broad-etreet, E.C.

Dulness is the prevailing condition of the Stock Markets in every department. Home, foreign, and miscellaneous securities are all at a standstill. This is due to various causes, the principal being the fortnightly settlement which commenced on Monday and closed on Wednesday. The volume of business transacted during the past fortnight was not large, but at the same time it was solid, and the result was a marked Improvement in prices on the previous settle- ment. Various Home rails exhibit a firmness in spite of prevailing dulness, among such being the Lancashire and Yorkshire, which have been purchased on the strength of the recent incr.ase in traffic returns.

A Railway Company which acquired a contract from the Portuguese Government to construct a line from Dslagoa was recently formed to connect the Transvaal with D-elagoa Bay. the immense advantage of which there was no ques- tion, and the capital of the company was immediately sub- acribed. Some interested parties, in endeavouring to spoil the company, started a report that the Portuguese Govern- ment had not granted a concession. Whereupon a report was immediately despatched by :be Portuguese Ministry to its English representative confirming the concession. In the meantime one or two professional men saw a chance, and issued a circular to the bondholders stating that there was misrepresentation in the prospectus, and inviting them to attend a meeting of botdholders on the 3 at nit. Thil meeting toek place, but a greater fiasco could not be im- agined. The convener of the meeting was unable to estab- lish a single allegation against the company, and the bond- holders present passed a resolution condemnatory of the convener of the meeting, and stigmatizing it as an attempt to wreck the company. I mention this meeting because the scheme itself is not only an important one, but to show how easy it is for interested parties, under the appearance uf acting for clients, ruining the success of really bona fide undertakings, or at any rate making them unmarketable; in this instance the company will benefit by the extra support that such action is likely to call forth.

div.head: UNION CHURCH, FRODSHAM : OPENING SERVICES.
div.p: UNION CHURCH, FRODSHAM : OPENING SERVICES.

The Union Church, Frodsham Bridge, was opened for Divine worship on Sunday last, when the Rev. J. Yonge, of Warrington, preached marring and evening to good con- gregations, whilst in the afternoon Mr. Gerrard Ford, of Manchester, conducted a service. The more formal opening of the sacred edifice took place on Thursday. Mr. T. Hux- ley, of Malpas, was the general contractor for the work The brickwork was carried out by Mr. George Davies. of F:odeham, and Messrs. Lea and Son, of Runcorn, construc- ted the heating apparatun on the high pressure System. A statement, read by Mr. Rigby, will be found below.

On Thursday afternoon the chapel was well filled by a congregation gathered to listen to a sermon by the Rev. Alexander Mac Kennel, of Bowdon, chairman of the Congre- gational Union. The reverend gentleman preached from the text I. Cm., iii., 21, 22, and 23rd verses. After the service tea was provided in Mr. Thomas Rigby's mill. There were about 300 persons present, and the tables were presided over by the following ladies :—Mrs. Jackson, Mrs. Wilkinson, Miss Wilkinson, Miss Rigby, Miss Wright, Miss Lovett, Mrs. Bowdon Mrs. Dobson, Mrs. Entwistle, Miss Moores, Miss Gibson, Turton, Miss Ormerod, and Miss J. Rigby. Subsequently a public meeting was held in the chapel under the presidency of Mr. Abraham Haworth, of Bowdon. Ladies and gentlemen from all parts of the country were present, the building being comfortably filled. On the platform were the Revs. A. McLaren, D.D., of Manchester, A. MacKennal, and H. Ward Price; and Messrs. S. Rigby, J.P. (Chester) and T. Rigby. Amongst the audience were the Boys. J. D. Thomas and E. Hall (of Runcorn), and the Rev. R. Yeatman, cf Widnee. Mr. T. Rigby read a report which stated that the services that day had been the outgrowth of the natural action of the free and voluntary churches of our land. Three or four families of Nonconformists, Baptist, and Congrega- tional having settled there a few years ago agreed to unite in conducting services for the public worship of God after the simple forms to which they had been accustomed, to conduct the teaching of children in Sunday schools, and to co-operate as churches of their order did in such works of benevolence and charity as came to their hands. They furnished a room in the neighbouring corn mill, and ob- tained the kelp of teachers both lay and clerical from the two denominations on Sundays in conducting public worship, and themselves conducted the teaching of the Sunday school, the distribution of tracts and the guidance of sewing meetings and mothers' meetings and other helpful agencies to the poor. They had continued this work for eight years, increasing in numbers and having many en- couraging testimonials to the acceptance of their work, they had erected this chapel for God's worship and these schools for the teaching of the children who came to them in religious truth, in humble trust that they might be honoured of God by His manifested approval and Benediction. Though only two-thirds of the cost had yet been raised, they had an assured faith that the other third would come in their Father's good time. The chapel, which would seat 180 people, and the schools and class rooms, that could accommodate from 300 to 400 children, with the adjacent outbuildings, stables, sheds, and boundary walls, had cost £1,518. The land, which is freehold, with the requisite preparations, had cost £3OO, and other incidental expenses would raise the cost to about £1,850. Payment for the land was made by the united efforts of the ladies of the congregation, and by a small bazaar and sewing meeting; and £l,OOO had been subscribed and paid on account to the builder. Upwards of £350 of this was contributed by generous friends of their principles outside the neighbour- hood, including some noble sums from the chairman and a few kindred friends, for which they were very grateful. They had the collectiens of Sunday, which amounted to £44, and of that afternoon, which amounted to £254e 10d, towards the balance. That morning's post brought him (Mr Rigby) a donation of £2O, a second con- tribution of a like sum from an old friend of the past, and there were others coming. They bespoke renewed generosity, with hope and earnest desire as they had set themselves the task of paying off the debt before they invited a minister to take pastoral over- sight of the church. With a church of nearly 40 members, a Sunday school of upwards of 180 scholars, and a large and increasing population that required teaching, and the benefitial influences of religion infusing into their daily life above everything else theyagaira commended their work to Their sympathy and prayer. (Applause). The Chairman concluded an address in which he con- gratulated tho'e present on the success of their labours, and drew attention to the fact that John Bunyan was the first preacher of a Union Church 250 years ago, by offering to give an additional donation of £5O to the building fund if Mr. Rigby could inform him at the end of six months that enly that amount was required to wipe off the debt. (Applause.) Dr. McLaren after a few words of conzratulation said the Congretational Union and the Baptist Union had come to

• LATEST . NEWS The death is announced from New York of John Godfrey Saxe, the American poet. The Irish Government have abandoned the prosecution against Messrs. Dillon, O'Brien' and others. Two houses fa Prescot-road, Liverpool, were burnt down on Friday morning. The inmates narrowly escaped, and only got out partially dressed. A Killarney telegram reports the arrest of seven men in addition to those already in ct.stody, charged with the murder of a man named Morphy near that town. THE KAPIINDA DISASTER.—A summons was granted at Bow-street. London, on Friday, on the application of the Board of Trade, against the captain of the Ada Melmore for an alleged infringement of the regulations for preventing collisions at sea. Replying to the workmen's deputation, on Friday after- noon, Lord Salisbury promised to consnit his colleagues with regard to a request that Government should assist in passing the Deceased Wife's r-ister Bill through the House of Lords. He did not, however, hold out any hope of pass- ing it. THE Lorenox CORPORATION INQUIRY.—The Select Com- mittee on the London Corporation inquiry re-assembled on Friday.—Mr. Johnson, secretary of the Metropolitan Rate- payers Association, said he received frequent payments from Sir Thomas Nelson, city solicitor, to organise opposi- tion to the London Government Bill.

THE STORM—FOUR MEN DROWNED. The storm of Thursday night has done a great deal of damage to shipping; and several crews were saved by life- boats. Snow fell in London on Friday morning. The fishing smack John and AgnPs, of St. Monanch, put into the Tyne fer refuge on Friday morning, her master report- ing that when off Ferne Island she experienced terrific weather. The smack was struck by a heavy sea, which carried five of the crew overboard, four of whom were drowned.

WRECK OF A STEAMER OFF NEWFOUNDLAND. SUPPOSED LOSS OF 200 LIVES. NEW YORK, THURSDAY.—lntelligence has been received , here that Messrs. Bowring Brother's screw steamship Eagle, which wri!; engaged in the seal fishing, has run upon the shoals near Funk Island, off Bonavista Bay, Newfoundland, and has become a total loss. The boiler is believed to have burst, and it is feared that the whole crew, numbering 200 men, was lost. A portion of the wreckage has been found upon the ice. The vessel belonged te St. John's. Sr. JOHN'S THIIRSDAY.—The latest reports received here tend to remove all doubt as to the fate of the sealing steamer Eagle. She was a vessel of 340 tons, arid sailed from this port with the sealing fleet on the 10th inst for Bonavista Bay, which lies one hundred miles north of St. John's She had a crew of thout 260 men on board, but the exact number is unknown. They were mostly married, and lived in the vicinity of St. John's. The vnourning in the city is general. This is the first crew of a sealing steamer having been lost on this coast, and the loss of life is the greatest known for many years piet.

From inquiries which were made at Liverpool, it appears that the Eagle was under the command of Captain Jack- man, and of the 200 hands on board over 130 of them were Nowfoundlanders, whose special functien is to capture the seals.

AMERICAN SYMPATHY WITH IRELAND. NEW YORK, THURSDAY —The Tammany Hall General Committee, the City Council of Chicago and the Lower Houses of the Colorado and Pennsylvanian Legislatures have adopted resolutions condemning coercion and expressing sympathy for Ireland. THE ATIEMPE ON THE LIFE OF THE CZAR.

BERLIN, FRlDAY.—lotelliTen-c; received here from St. Petersburg fully confirms the news that an attempt was made on the life of the Czar. On Tuesday last his Majesty was fired at in the park at Gatchina by an officer, but luckily escaped uninjured, although the arm was discharged at close quarters. The would-be assassin has sines been arrested.
ARRIVAL OF THE QUEEN AT CANNES. CANives, FRIDAY, 10 AM.—The Qmeen, accompanied by Prince and Princess Henry of Battenburg and suite, has jest arrived here.

CANNES, FRIDAY, 10-30 AM—The Queen was received at the railway station by the Duke of Edinburgh and Prince George of Wales, the Prefect of the Alps Maritimes, the Mayor of Cannes, the 13ritish Consul at Nice, and the British Vice-Consul here.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

A model of the Manchester Ship Canal, 401 t. long and Oft. wide, was gxhibited on Wednesday at the Manchester Royal Exchange, and secured a great deal of attention from the members. It is placed in that part of the building where gentlemen con- nected with the iron trade usually assemble for business purposes. Mr. E. Leader Williams was very busy on Wednesday in giving information to the crowds who gathered round him of the works which will, it is hoped, be started in May, and of which he is, in a sense, the father. The model will ultimately be shown at the Exhibition at Old Traf- ford. Before the Exhibition opens, however, if will be on view for some time at the Royal ,institu- tion. The scale is a foot to the mile, but for pur- poses of relief the elevation has been slightly in- creased. Every feature of the country between Manchester and Liverpool is represented, even to stray fences along the banks of the Canal. Docks, locks, turnbridges, railway crossings, estuary em- bankments, and many other details of the works are shown; ordnance plans and Ship Canal surveys having been most carefully transcribed. The estuary of the Mersey is shown at low water, spring tide. The model is in wood. 1

An important private meeting of members of the Salford Town Jouncil and others interested in the Manchester Ship Canal Company was held on Tues- day, by the invitation of the Mayor of Salford (Alderman Farmer). A resolution congratulating the directors of the Canal Company upon the pros- pect of the speedy realization of the enterprise, and strongly urging the inhabitants of the borough to take up shares, was carried unanimously. A com- mittee was appointed to take action in assisting the directors to raise the capital, and shares amounting to several thousands of pounds were subscribed during the meeting. A determined effort is to be made in Oldham in support of the Manchester Ship Canal scheme, and the Mayor has convened a meeting of the leading commercial men and representatives of limited companies to further the project. His Worship states that he is convinced that benefit would accrue to the trade of the town by the formation of the canal, and he hopes those attending the meeting will be prepared to state what their firms or companies would do in the matter of taking up shares.

It is stated that shares are being taken up rapidly, and that there is a good prospect of the Prince of Wales being called upon to cut the first sod, after opening the Jubilee Exhibition at Man- chester.

div.head: LOCAL TOWNSHIP MEETINGS.
div.p: LOCAL TOWNSHIP MEETINGS.
LATCHFORD.

On Monday morning the annual meeting of the rate- payers of Latchford was held at the Norton Arms Hotel, Mr William Fairhurst, one of the overseers, presiding. There were also present the Rev A. Kenworthy, and Messrs W. Pierpoint, E. Greenali, jun., H. Greenal I, J. Taylor, Turner, J. W. Booth, J. Shaw Green, and W. S. Hawkins (assistant overseer).—Mr. W. Pierpoint asked bow it was that Mr. John Lunt, who was nominated with Mr. William Fairhurst at the last meeting as overseer, bad not served during the year, Mr. James Moore having been appointed to the office by the magistrates, and it was stated in reply that Mr. Lunt did not want the office, and that the appointment of over- seers was a matter that was entirely in the hands of the magistrates. Soon afterwards Mr. Lunt attended the meeting, and, after a little discussion, he consented to accept office. He and Mr William Nairhurst were then nominated as overseers for the ensuing year.—The annual statement of accounts, which was adopted, showed that there was in the bank at the commencement of the half year the sum of £509 103 sd, and £389 Os 8d had been returned from the poor-rate, chc., making a total of £1,478 lie Id. The expen- diture had been £897 ltla 9d, leaving a balance in the bank of £5BO 14s 4d.—Messrs Edward Greenall. jun., and John Lee were, at the request of Mr 11 Greenall, appointed col- lectors of tithes for the township.—Mr H Greenall, who ap- peared on behalf of the Rector of Grappenball, said he should collect the tithes for them as their solicitor, and whatever remuneration was give would be given by the Rector. The collectors would pay the gross sum received over to the Rector.—The meeting terminated with a vote of thanks to the Chairman:

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

On Friday evening last weeVa-m—eeting of the inhatitants contributing to the highway rates of the highway parish of Warrington was held at the King and Queen Inn, Padgate- lane, for the purpose of "receiving and considering the accounts of the waywarden ; appointing a waywarden for the ensuing year. and sanctioning the appointment by such waTwardan, and fixing the remuneration of a collector of highway rates." Mr. John Grounds (waywarden) presided. There was a small attendance. Mr. J. L. Tunstall (assis- tant overseer for Warrington) made a statement with refer- ence to the accounts, from which we give the following. items :—Receipts : From rate,•£s39 2s sd; other sources, £26 18s 641; total, £566 Os 11d. Payments: Treasurer of Highway Board, £541 Os 6d; other payments, £25 Os sd; total, £566 03 ltd. The accounts were p.l.esed. Mr. John Grounds was re-apoointed wavwarden for the ensuing year. The remuneration of the collector of highway rates (Mr. Tanstall) was fixed at £23; and a vote of thanks having been accorded to Mr. Grounds for presiding, the meeting was brought to a conclusion. BOLD.

The annual vestry meeting in connection with the town- ship of Bold was held at the Tipping Arms Inn the other evening. There was a good attendance, the chair being occupied by Mr. W. W. Tipping. The following were nominated for tbe two vacant posts of overseers : Messrs. James Baker and Thomas Whitfield (retiring over- seers), and J. R. Whalley, George Swift, and W. Johnston. Their names will be submitted to the St. Helens magistrates on the 4th prox. Mr. J. Newton was'unanimossly re-elected highway warden. At the conclusion ,of the other business the chairman proposed that as this is the Jubilee year, it should be commemorated in the township by the improve- ment and adornment of the school playground, towards which object he would subscribe £lO. The preposition was cordially received by the meeting, and £2O was subscribed off band. The following were appointed a committee to carry out the project :—Messrs. A. T. Johnstone (secretary), T. Baker, W. W. Tipping, T. Whitfield, J. Newton, J. Davies, and J. Baker.

div.head: ..-,-...ui........-.
div.p: Some excitement has been created by the discovery that at a London district post office a supposed " infernal ma- chine "lead been addressed to Mr. Balfour, Chief Secretary , for Ireland. The mntents of the " machine have under- gone chemical analysis, but the result has not transpired. DEPARTURE OF TEE QUEEN FOR TNE CONTINENT.— The Queen, accompanied by Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg, left Windsor on Tuesday for Portsmouth, on her way to the continent. The morning was sunny, and a number of persons assembled on the road to the station to sce her Majesty depart. The Royal train arrived at Ports- mouth at noon. On the train arriving on the amth rail- way jetty, alongside which the Royal yacht Victoria and Albert wag lying, her Majesty alighted, and was received by Admiral Sir George Willis and staffs. The Victoria:and Albert got under weigh shortly before one o'clock, and the marine guard on board the flagship gave a royal salute, whilst the Admiral's band played the National Anthem.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met S-t-f;u-r—o'CiOck.:

MISCELLANEOI79.—EarI eiDOGAN, replying to Lord Brad- bourne, said the equitable jurisdiction clauses of the pro- posed Irish Land Bill would be limited in their application to holdings of land not exceeding fity pounds.—The Church Pato6nage Bill was read a third time, and passed.—The Railway and Canal Rates Bill and the Sheriffs and County Court Bill passed through Committee.—The Army Annual Bill .was read a second time.
The House adjourned it nine, o'clock until the 12th HOUSE' OF COMMONS.
The House met at four o'clock.

QIIESTIONS.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQI7EIt, re- plying to Mr. King, said income tax was levied in this country on all incomes, irrespective of tbe source from where they were obtained.—Sir J. FERGUSON, replying to Sir G. Campbell, said the Egyptian land tax had not been reduced but rearranged.—Mr. W. H. Surrii, replying to Mr. T. Healy, said the Government regarded the passing of the Land Bill introduced in the House of Lords as vital to the existence of the Government, and every effort would be used to pass the bill into law.—Sir J. FERGUSON intimated that no information had been received relative to the repor- ted attempt on the life of the Cztr.—Mr. W. H. SMITH intimated that if leave was given to introduce the Criminal Law Amendment Bill to-night the Government would not ask for the second reading until Tuesday. The Government would allow a week between the second reading and the committee stage.

THE CROFTEBS.—Dr.Aux, by leave, moved the ad- journment of the House, and stated the pressing need of more diligent action of the Crofter Commission to get fair rents fixed, and against proceedings in bankruptcy involv- ing the expulsion of the crofters from their holdings before applications to fix rents could be heard. The Commis- sioners had only given six decisions in six months; he urged the appointment of assistant commissioners and valuers.—Mr. A. Basottrt admitted the defect in the Crofter's Act, but he could not stop important Irish busi- ness to remedy it.—Mr. J. CHAMBERLAIN suggested that the , Government might, if no opposition was raised, introduce a short bill to remedy the defect.—Mr. A. BALFOUR. said con- sideration should be given to such suagestion.—The motion for the adjournment of the House was negatived. THE COERCION BILL.

The adjourned debate on the motion for leave to introduce the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill was resumed. —Mr. PARNELL said it was not until last night that they had been put in complete possession in all their nakedness and dishonesty of the Government proposals for Ireland, and the information showed the gravity of the conspiracy that existed between the Tory party and the Liberal Unionists to coerce tenants into payment of impossible rents and to secure purchase of landlords' interest at exor- bitant prices. He contended that crime had diminished to such an extent that it could not with truth be urged as justification for coercion. He concluded by moving, as an amendment to 'he motion for leave to introduce the bill, "that the House immedi- ately resolve itself into committee to consider the state of Ireland."—The Imes SECRETARY opposed the amendment, and defended the Government proposals.—Mr. BIZADLAUGH said he never heard a more contemptible cue made ent for passing a permanent coercion bill.

div.p: [LEFT sirrixo.

Tuesday night's "Gazette" contained a Royal proclama- tion prohibiting the importation of all coins coined in any foreign country, other than gold or silver coins. The Prince and Princess of Wales, with two of their daughters, visited Bloomsbary-square, London, on Wednes• day, to open the new building of the College of Precep- tors.
James Fook Finnemore was committed for trial on Tues- day, at Worship-street Police Court, London, for the wilful murder of his wife, at Finsbury, by stabbing her with a table knife.

There are signs that the strike of weavers at Ashton, which has lasted for sixteen weeks, is approaching a ter- mination. It is now asserted that weavers are going back to work individually at the old rate of wages. The General Steam Navigation Company's steamer Hol- landia was sunk in the Thames on Thursday through a collision with the Peninsular and Oriental steamer Ancona. The latter returned to Gravesend for repairs. THE HOXTON MURDER—The trial of Thomas William Carrell for the murder of Lydia Green, at Hoxton, was con- tiued at the Old Bailey, on Tharsday. Thomas Attrell, a lodger at Mrs. Green's house, said he met the prisoner about 1 seven o'clock on the morning of the murder. They went to I a public-house and the prisoner borrowed witness's latchkey. —Annie Manton, employed at the same place as the deceased, deposed to giving the prisoner the deceased's wages on the afternoon of the murder.—The trial was further adjourned. On Friday the trial was resumed, when the evidence for the prosecution was continued.
